109-1-LB27_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB27_Intro_Copy.docx LB27 amends the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act and the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund statutes. It (1) authorizes the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund (held by the State Treasurer and invested by the state investment officer) to be used to finance loan repayments under the Rural Health Act and directs investment earnings to the General Fund beginning October 1, 2024; (2) restates Act purposes and creates the Nebraska Rural Health Advisory Commission; (3) revises eligibility and award limits, adding a dentist-specific loan‑repayment option (dentists with <5 years’ practice/no prior assistance) allowing up to $60,000/year for up to five years (max $300,000) with DHHS making payments directly and agreements exempt from the State Procurement Act; and (4) expresses legislative intent to appropriate $1.5 million from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to the Department of Health and Human Services for FY2025‑26 for these dentist loan repayments. Creates a DHHS loan repayment program for dentists who treat Medicaid patients, administered by the "department" and subject to terms set by the "commission." Eligible dentists must have practiced <5 years and not previously received Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act assistance. Agreements (exempt from the State Procurement Act) require five years' practice in Nebraska and a commission‑specified Medicaid patient percentage. DHHS may pay recipients up to $60,000 per year (to $300,000 max) for qualified educational debt for up to five years; recipients must document use of funds. Breach triggers repayment of all funds plus 8% simple interest; obligations cancel on death/total permanent disability. DHHS may only use specifically appropriated funds. Legislature intends to appropriate $1.5 million from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to DHHS for FY2025‑26. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB280_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB280_Intro_Copy.docx LB280 amends Nebraska gaming statutes to (1) expand the duties and authorities of the State Racing and Gaming Commission to implement the new audit provisions in section 7; (2) require each authorized gaming operator to obtain, at its expense, an annual independent CPA audit (including internal control report) and submit it electronically to the Auditor of Public Accounts and the Racing and Gaming Commission within six months (extensions allowed by the Auditor); and (3) give the Auditor of Public Accounts authority to review those audit reports for errors or deficiencies, examine operators’ books, records, funds, and accounts as prescribed, and report findings electronically to the Governor, Legislature, and gaming commission. The Racing and Gaming Commission’s Racetrack Gaming Fund (license/application fees) is explicitly authorized to be used for administration and for any audit, examination, or review required or authorized under section 7. The fund’s investment remains with the state investment officer; investment earnings are credited to the General Fund. Adds an annual audit requirement for each authorized gaming operator: operators must pay for an independent certified public accountant (licensed in Nebraska) to audit annual financial statements and internal controls covering all Nebraska operations. Audit reports must be submitted electronically within six months after fiscal year‑end to the Auditor of Public Accounts (APA) and the gaming commission, unless the APA grants a written extension. The APA will review audits for mathematical errors, improper accounting, or deficiencies—particularly those affecting gross gaming revenue or gaming tax—and report results electronically to the Governor, the Legislature, and the gaming commission. 109-1-LB281_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB281_Intro_Copy.docx LB281 revises Nebraska nursing regulation. The State Board of Health retains appointment responsibilities, including geographic representation. The Board's duties are harmonized and expressly include administration of the Nurse Licensure Compact; the department is authorized to report personal identifying information (including social security numbers) to the compact’s coordinated licensure information system. The bill removes qualifications and duties for a separate Board of Advanced Practice Registered Nurses and repeals sections 38-205, 38-206, and 38-2307. 109-1-LB285_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB285_Intro_Copy.docx LB285 amends Nebraska law to prohibit the marketing, sale, and Tax Commissioner certification of flavored electronic nicotine delivery systems (defined by taste/smell or manufacturer claims). 109-1-LB287_Intro Governor Veto Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB287_Intro_Copy.docx LB287 amends the Nebraska Housing Agency Act to impose specific bed‑bug duties on housing agencies for cities of the metropolitan class. Agencies must visually inspect units before renting, refuse to show/rent vacant units known or reasonably suspected to be infested, disclose adjacent-unit infestation/treatment status, and upon complaint: acknowledge within five days, secure investigatory services from a pest control professional (licensed under the Pesticide Act) within five days, remediate confirmed infestations within 14 days, inspect adjacent units, provide advance notice before unit entry and timely notice of pest‑control determinations, and keep two years of written records (including chemicals used). The housing agency is made financially responsible for investigation and remediation costs. The bill repeals the prior version of section 71-1572. Makes the housing agency for a city of the metropolitan class responsible for bed‑bug prevention and response. Defines "bed bug" and "pest control professional" (a commercial applicator licensed under the Pesticide Act). Requirements include pre‑rental visual inspections, prohibition on renting units known or reasonably suspected to be infested, disclosure of adjacent unit treatments, and specific complaint timelines: acknowledge complaints within 5 days, inspect or hire a licensed pest control professional within 5 days, remediate within 14 days if infestation is confirmed, inspect adjacent units, provide tenant notices, and keep written records (including chemicals used) for two years. Fiscal effect: the housing agency is explicitly made responsible for the costs of investigation and remediation; no separate appropriation is provided. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB289_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB289_Final_Copy.docx LB289 modifies statutes governing villages and municipal economic development. Key agency references and operational changes:\n\n- County board: must accept incorporation petitions that now designate whether a new village board will have three or five trustees and will appoint three or five initial trustees at incorporation.\n- County canvassing board: completes canvass of village incorporation and later trustee-number elections.\n- Election commissioner or county clerk: receives petitions/resolutions to submit trustee-number questions (petitions require signatures from at least 5% of registered village electors, filed ≥70 days before a general election); conducts election and canvass.\n- Village clerk: provides petition forms and assists with petition procurement.\n- Village board of trustees and city councils (first and second class): may, by ordinance, serve as the board of adjustment (decisions require a two-thirds vote of the body).\n- Local Option Municipal Economic Development Act: redefines “qualifying business” to expressly include retail trade (with a statutory definition).\n\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. Adds procedures allowing village voters to choose whether their board of trustees has three or five members via petition or board resolution submitted for a statewide general election. Key agencies: village clerk (issues petitions), election commissioner or county clerk (assists with petitions, accepts filings at least 70 days before the election, places the question on the ballot, and gives notice), and the county canvassing board (conducts the canvass and finalizes results). Petitions must equal at least 5% of registered village electors from the prior statewide general election and be verified per section 32-631. Vote outcomes trigger statutory procedures: increasing to five invokes sections 32-568/32-569 (vacancies), decreasing to three invokes section 17-202. Municipal applications must state the amount requested and describe the project. The Department will consider applications in receipt order and may approve grants only within available appropriations; individual grants are capped at $5 million. 109-1-LB29_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB29_Intro_Copy.docx LB29 amends the Administrative Procedure Act to require state agencies to review all existing and pending rules and regulations beginning January 1, 2026 and every three years thereafter. Each agency head must designate an oversight individual. Agencies must file detailed electronic reports to the Clerk of the Legislature by June 30 in review years addressing necessity for public health/safety/welfare, cost–benefit, effectiveness measurement, consideration of less‑restrictive alternatives, and whether rules derive from state statute, federal mandate, or court order. The Legislative Reference Committee will refer reports to appropriate standing committees, which must report back to the Clerk by December 15 with any legislative recommendations. Agency rulemaking is suspended during the review except for rules affecting health/safety/welfare, time‑sensitive rules, or those subject to statutory deadlines. Section 84‑920 is amended to incorporate this section into the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes are included. Beginning Jan. 1, 2026, every state agency must review all existing and pending rules and regulations and repeat reviews every three years. Each agency head must designate an oversight designee. Agencies must file an electronic, detailed report and supporting documents with the Clerk of the Legislature by June 30 in review years addressing: necessity for public health/safety/welfare; cost‑benefit; effectiveness measurement; consideration of less‑restrictive alternatives; and whether the rule stems from state statute, federal mandate, or court order. The Legislative Reference Committee will refer reports to appropriate standing committees, which must return electronic committee reports with legislative or clarification recommendations to the Clerk by Dec. 15. Rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act is suspended during reviews except for rules affecting health/safety/welfare, time‑sensitive rules, or those bound by statutory deadlines. 109-1-LB300_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB300_Intro_Copy.docx LB300 amends state statutes to expand and operationalize the Superintendent Pay Transparency Act. It requires boards of education (Class I–V school districts) and boards of educational service units (ESUs) to set superintendent and ESU administrator compensation in compliance with the Act. Key provisions: defines benefit, compensation, salary, and beginning-teacher compensation; caps superintendent/administrator total compensation at five times the district’s or ESU’s beginning-teacher compensation; treats cross-payments between districts and ESUs as compensation of the paying entity; invalidates contracts exceeding the cap and requires forfeiture and return of excess pay and a notice to the Commissioner of Education within 30 days. Boards must publish proposed contracts/amendments, cost estimates, and the statutory maximum at least three days before consideration and post approved contracts and cost estimates within two days (website publication allowed). Adds definitions and limits under the Superintendent Pay Transparency Act affecting school districts, educational service units (ESUs), school boards, and superintendents/administrators. Key points:\n- Defines "benefit," "compensation," "salary," and "compensation for a beginning teacher," and explicitly includes employer retirement and insurance contributions (School Employees Retirement Act; Class V School Employees Retirement Act) and tax-deferred plans (IRC §§125, 403(b), 457).\n- Prohibits contracts that would pay a superintendent or ESU administrator more than five times the district/ESU beginning-teacher compensation for the same year; dual compensation is attributed to the employing district/ESU.\n- Violating contracts are invalid; excess pay must be forfeited and returned to the district/ESU, and a notice must be filed with the Commissioner of Education within 30 days.\n- No new appropriations or funding increases are made. 109-1-LB313_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB313_Intro_Copy.docx LB313 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§48-118 and 48-118.04 (Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act). It affirms that an employer or the workers' compensation insurer is subrogated to an injured employee’s third-party claim and may recover amounts beyond compensation paid. Recoveries in excess of compensation, after deducting recovery expenses, must be paid promptly to the employee or dependents and treated as an advance on future compensation. For third‑party settlements, written agreement of the employee (or representative) and the employer’s workers’ compensation insurer (or employer if uninsured) or court approval is required. If distribution is disputed, the court must (after recovery expenses) pay one-third to the employee, then satisfy employer/insurer compensation payments (paid or owed), and remit any remaining balance to the employee. No specific state agency funding or appropriations are addressed. Added text sets a priority scheme for distribution of recovered funds after deducting reasonable recovery expenses: (1) one‑third of the remainder to the employee (or personal representative); (2) from the balance left, the employer or workers' compensation insurer is reimbursed for compensation already paid or that it may be obligated to pay in the future; (3) any remaining balance then goes to the employee (or personal representative). No government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no changes to appropriations, funding, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB317_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB317_Final_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services, Department of Agriculture, Department of Banking and Finance, Department of Economic Development, Department of Insurance, Department of Labor, Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Revenue, Department of Transportation, Department of Veterans' Affairs, Military Department LB317 reallocates duties, funds, and statutory roles among state agencies. It transfers appropriations and salary limits from the Department of Natural Resources to the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment, treats DNR staff as transferred, and requires the Department of Administrative Services (DAS) to certify unpaid DNR obligations as valid encumbrances. DAS’s budget administrator directs multiple statutory fund transfers (notably $1,000,000 from the Water Resources Cash Fund to the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Cash Fund by June 30, 2025 and other Water Sustainability Fund transfers) and a $200,000 transfer from the Clean‑burning Motor Fuel Development Fund; DAS also manages warrants, purchasing preferences, rebate review, and a public contract database. The Department of Agriculture gains expanded pesticide regulatory and enforcement authority (fines up to $5,000) and reimbursement powers from the Pesticide Administrative Cash Fund, hosts the Riparian Vegetation Task Force, and oversees certain weights‑and‑measures approvals. DHHS is added to several boards/committees, may participate in groundwater hearings, and may receive forfeited sureties for site care. DOT, DED, and Revenue are named stakeholders for flood/infrastructure planning; Revenue administers ethanol tax credits and a new Litter Fee Collection Fund. Banking & Finance, Insurance, Labor, Motor Vehicles, Veterans’ Affairs, Correctional Services, and the Military Department are added as official recipients of session law distributions and receive limited statutory references (appointments/exemptions). Creates a July 1, 2025 merger of the Department of Natural Resources into the Department of Environment and Energy, renaming it the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment and creating a Governor‑appointed, Legislature‑confirmed Chief Water Officer (reports to the Director). DNR positions transfer to the new department with continuous service and retained personnel/bargaining rights; existing DNR rules remain effective. 109-1-LB338_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB338_Intro_Copy.docx LB338 (introduced to the Legislature’s Banking, Commerce and Insurance Committee by Sen. Wordekemper) prohibits life insurers, disability insurers, and long-term care insurers from using genetic information to determine eligibility, set premiums, or impose preexisting-condition exclusions absent a clinical diagnosis. It bars insurers from soliciting or considering genetic test results or an individual’s decision to undergo genetic testing. Allowed exceptions: insurers may review medical records for clinical diagnoses, ask about family history, and rely on clinical diagnoses for coverage decisions. The bill cites the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (29 U.S.C. §1182) and uses the definitions in Neb. Rev. §48‑236. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds findings citing the Legislature and the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (29 U.S.C. 1182) and prohibits life, group disability, and long‑term care insurers—absent a clinical diagnosis—from cancelling, limiting, denying coverage, setting premium differentials, soliciting or using genetic information or test results, or considering a person's decision about genetic testing. Exceptions allow insurers to review medical records during underwriting, ask about family history, and rely on clinical diagnoses in medical records. Definitions reference section 48‑236. No state agencies or departments beyond the Legislature are newly created or named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB340_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB340_Intro_Copy.docx LB340 enacts the Asbestos Trust Claims Transparency Act and the Asbestos Claims Priorities and Over‑Naming Reform Act, amending Neb. Rev. Stat. §25‑224. Key government-related provisions:\n\n- Nebraska courts: empowered to order claimants to file additional asbestos trust claims, produce trust governance materials and affidavits, delay trials (minimum 90 days) after compliance, hold evidentiary hearings on prima facie medical proof, and consolidate certain asbestos cases for trial.\n- Discovery and evidentiary rules: courts may permit defendants to subpoena or seek discovery from asbestos trusts; trust claim materials and trust governance documents are admissible and not privileged.\n- Judgment effects: courts must apply setoffs to defendants for amounts claimants have or will receive from trusts.\n- Statute of limitations: §25‑224 amended to toll non‑malignant asbestos claims until diagnosis meeting the act’s prima facie standards or death.\n\nNo state agency appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations are included. The additions create two named acts governing asbestos litigation: the Asbestos Trust Claims Transparency Act and the Asbestos Claims Priorities and Over‑Naming Reform Act. They require claimants to file all asbestos trust claims, produce trust‑claim materials and affidavits, allow courts to compel filings, make trust documents admissible (not privileged), permit defendants discovery from trusts (with claimant cooperation), and authorize judgment setoffs for trust recoveries. They set strict medical‑evidence standards (qualified physician reports, AMA Guides, American Thoracic Society standards), limit discovery until a prima facie showing is made, allow limited consolidation, and toll certain statutes of limitations. No federal or state agencies or departments are specifically named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. DOCX | PDF

The bill preserves specified exemptions, allows the board advisory hearings on supplier termination of construction/acquisition, and maintains injunctive enforcement for violations. For privately developed renewable facilities, the executive director may notify private electric suppliers by certified mail and assess a $500 fine if construction began less than 30 days before required notice; suppliers may request a board hearing, and the board can require cessation or assess hearing costs. 109-1-LB34_Final Final Reading Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB34_Final_Copy.docx LB34 revises Nebraska time statutes and related state employment leave provisions. It: (1) authorizes adoption of year‑round daylight saving/standard time (central = UTC−5; mountain = UTC−6) once authorized by federal law or order and after three adjacent states adopt identical measures; (2) makes current daylight‑saving dates null when that change becomes operative; (3) preserves election poll hours by time zone; and (4) standardizes sick‑ and vacation‑leave accounting to 11:59 p.m. central time and retains administrative provisions assigning rulemaking to the Director of Personnel. The bill names the Governor (for leave extensions), the Executive Board of the Legislative Council (for legislative employees), employing agencies, and the Public Employees Retirement Board (retirement treatment of leave cashouts). No appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations are included. Adds a state standard-time provision: Nebraska would set standard time at UTC‑5 in the central zone and UTC‑6 in the mountain zone. It defines “Coordinated Universal Time” as the scale maintained by the General Conference on Weights and Measures and interpreted/modified for the U.S. by the U.S. Secretary of Commerce in coordination with the U.S. Secretary of the Navy. The subsection becomes operative only after (1) authorization by U.S. law or an order of the U.S. Secretary of Transportation (or when no longer in conflict with such federal law/order) and (2) three adjacent states adopt a single year‑round time. The provision also becomes null and void if subsection (2) of section 49‑1301 becomes operative. No agencies are allocated funding and no appropriations or budget changes are made. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB361_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB361_Intro_Copy.docx LB361 amends the Nebraska Fair Employment Practice Act to (1) prohibit covered employers, including state and other governmental agencies, from discriminating or retaliating against individuals for reporting work‑related injuries, filing claims, or seeking remedies under the Nebraska Workers’ Compensation Act, and declares the Act’s remedies supplemental to workers’ compensation; (2) establish a right to jury trial in civil actions under the Act, explicitly applying this right to suits against state and governmental agencies; and (3) clarify that state and governmental agencies may be sued under the Act in the same manner as other employers. 109-1-LB366_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB366_Intro_Copy.docx Creates a Legislative Economic Analysis Unit and Chief Economist within the Legislature. Agencies (boards, commissions, departments, etc., excluding the Adjutant General's office, courts including the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Court, the Commission of Industrial Relations, the Legislature, and the Secretary of State as to specified duties) must publish and electronically submit proposed rules and supporting materials — including cost‑benefit analyses, job impacts, classification as major/nonmajor, related regulatory actions, and proposed effective dates — to the Legislature and the Chief Economist before filing with the Secretary of State. The Unit will report on major rules to the relevant legislative committee within 15 legislative days, assessing procedural compliance and regulatory impacts. Major rules cannot be published until ratified by the Legislature or after 60 legislative days without final vote; the Governor may approve emergency major rules with required findings. Courts may review whether statutory requirements for rule effect and major‑rule status were met. No funding or appropriation changes are included. Adds procedural controls involving: the Legislature; the Secretary of State; the Governor; the Chief Economist; the Legislative Economic Analysis Unit; courts; and any agency promulgating rules. Key points: within one month the Legislature must provide an electronic address for rule delivery; agencies must publish and electronically submit rule packages (copy, statement, major/nonmajor classification, related actions and economic effects, proposed effective date) to the Legislature and Chief Economist before filing with the Secretary of State; agencies must also submit cost‑benefit analyses including job impacts. The Legislative Economic Analysis Unit must report on major rules to the relevant committee within 15 legislative days assessing compliance and private‑sector impacts. Major rules cannot take effect or be published until ratified by law or after 60 legislative days unless expedited by the Governor with a public justification; courts may review compliance and major‑rule designation. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB367_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB367_Intro_Copy.docx LB367 amends the Uniform Credentialing Act to (1) prohibit credentialed providers under the Medicine and Surgery, Mental Health, Nurse, Pharmacy, and Psychology practice acts from delivering conversion therapy to persons under 19; (2) add provision of conversion therapy as a disciplinary ground under section 38-178; and (3) declare such conduct a deceptive trade practice under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The bill authorizes the department, with recommendation of the board, to deny, suspend, or revoke pharmacy technician registrations for violations now including conversion-therapy-related grounds, and preserves existing department procedures (notice, hearings, Licensee Assistance Program participation). It also bars expenditure of state or political-subdivision funds for conducting, referring for, or providing health-benefit coverage of conversion therapy. No specific appropriations or new budget allocations are made. Adds a ban on licensed health professionals (under the Medicine and Surgery, Mental Health, Nurse, Pharmacy, and Psychology Practice Acts) from providing "conversion therapy" to anyone under 19. Defines conversion, gender‑identity conversion, and sexual‑orientation conversion therapy. Violations are treated as deceptive trade practices under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Exempts clergy/religious counselors acting in a pastoral (non‑healthcare) capacity. Prohibits use of state funds or funds of any political subdivision to conduct, refer for, or provide health‑benefit coverage for conversion therapy. No new appropriations or allocations are made; instead the text forbids government spending for these services. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB368_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB368_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the Nebraska Youth in Care Bill of Rights and assigns implementation duties to the department and related actors. The department must facilitate joint-sibling placement or visitation, reunification and family visitation per state and federal law, inform children of reasons for denials, ensure confidentiality, provide transition plans (including for pregnant/parenting youth), and ensure access to identity and case documents. Caseworkers must be trained on and provide paper copies of rights, discuss them with youth (timing: within 72 hours and within two weeks of placement, then quarterly), and seek acknowledgments. Guardians ad litem must discuss rights within two weeks of appointment and every six months. Youth may file grievances with the department; the department must acknowledge receipt within three business days and advise on Administrative Procedure Act review. The Nebraska Strengthening Families Act Committee will monitor implementation. No appropriations or budget changes are specified. Added provisions impose duties on "the department" (the child welfare agency), caseworkers, court-appointed guardians ad litem, and the courts. Key agency responsibilities: facilitate sibling joint placement/visitation, reunification and family visitation, confidentiality and access to vital records, and provide transition plans for youth leaving foster care. Caseworkers must be trained on and provide written copies of youth rights, discuss them on set timelines (within 72 hours, two weeks, and quarterly), explain grievance procedures, and offer private opportunities to raise complaints. Guardians ad litem must review rights within two weeks and biannually and report infringements to the court. The department must acknowledge grievances within three business days and advise on Administrative Procedure Act review. The Nebraska Strengthening Families Act Committee (sec. 43-4716) will monitor implementation. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF

(2) A person under 19 who is committed to the Department of Correctional Services for secure care may consent to and make decisions regarding medical care, mental health services, and related services during commitment without parental consent, except as required by section 71-6902. The bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budget allocations. Adds that individuals 18+ may consent to their own health care unless in DHHS custody under a juvenile court order. 109-1-LB37_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB37_Intro_Copy.docx LB37 adopts the Railroad Safety Act (Secs. 1–9), amends Neb. Rev. The bill defines terms (referencing federal statutes/regulations and the Federal Railroad Administration for "main line"), requires wayside/hot-bearing detectors in definitions, bars operation of trains carrying hazardous substances longer than 8,500 feet on any state main line, and creates a civil-liability rule that plaintiffs injured by trains exceeding 7,000 feet may not have recovery reduced for comparative fault if length caused the harm. The Act excludes PSC authority over railroad labor relations. Operative date: July 1, 2026. No funding or appropriation changes. Adds definitions (including "Commission," defined as the Public Service Commission) and new safety requirements: railroads may not operate trains carrying hazardous substances over 8,500 feet on state main lines; if a train longer than 7,000 feet is found by a jury to have caused crash-related harm, a plaintiff's recovery cannot be reduced for comparative fault. The bill references the Federal Railroad Administration (timetable filings) and adds device/technology definitions (wayside detector systems, hot bearings detectors, dragging equipment detectors). It also clarifies the Act does not give the Public Service Commission jurisdiction over railroad labor relations. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

Stat. §25-21,185.11 to clarify the effect of releases, covenants not to sue, or similar agreements. A release still discharges the released party and precludes that party from being joined or—if already joined—provides grounds for dismissal, while that party's negligence remains subject to §25-21,185.09. 109-1-LB417_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB417_Intro_Copy.docx LB417 assigns the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska authority to administer the Nebraska Promise Program and enacts the College Promise Act. It creates a College Promise Fund administered by the Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education to reimburse community and state colleges for tuition waivers (eligible Nebraska residents with family income < $65,000, GPA ≥2.5; up to 2 years at community college or 4 years at state college). Colleges must waive remaining tuition after federal grants and state scholarships; the Legislature intends to fully fund the Fund annually equal to total waiver value. The state investment officer may invest idle Fund moneys per existing investment statutes. The bill also amends duties of the State Board of Education and State Department of Education (assessment, reporting, career‑readiness tests) and creates a Governor‑appointed technical advisory committee. An emergency clause makes the act effective upon approval. Added provisions identify the Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education as administrator of a new "College Promise Fund" to distribute money to Nebraska community colleges and state colleges; the fund will consist of legislative transfers and the Legislature intends to fully fund it each year equal to the total value of tuition waivers. The state investment officer may invest available fund balances under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. Community colleges/state colleges must verify eligibility, notify applicants within 45 days (with appeal rights through the Coordinating Commission), and waive 100% of remaining tuition after federal grants and state scholarships for eligible low‑income Nebraska residents. The State Board (and the Department) must recommend and implement career‑readiness assessments (free to 12th‑grade public students) and require school districts to report individual scores. 109-1-LB43_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB43_Final_Copy.docx LB43 amends Nebraska siting and notice requirements for electric generation and transmission. Key agency roles and changes:\n\n- Nebraska Power Review Board (the "board") and its executive director: owners must notify and certify to the board for facilities/transmission within a 10-mile radius of defined military installations that no electronic-related equipment/components are manufactured by a "foreign adversary." The act takes effect immediately. Adds requirements that electric suppliers and owners of generation or transmission facilities within 10 miles of specified U.S. Air Force sites (as defined by 31 C.F.R. 802.211(b)(3) and 802.227(c), regs as of Jan 1, 2025) must submit one‑time certifications to "the board" that their facilities contain no electronic equipment/components manufactured by a "foreign adversary" (as defined by 15 C.F.R. 791.4, as of Feb 7, 2025) and must notify the board if that changes. 109-1-LB440_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB440_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the Education Leave and Support Act, administered by the State Department of Education. Establishes a 0.35% payroll fee on taxable wages of certificated teachers effective Jan 1, 2026; employers collect the fee from employees, remit it quarterly to the State Treasurer, and remit an equal employer-match. Proceeds fund the newly created State Education Leave Fund, invested by the state investment officer under existing investment acts. The department will reimburse school districts (beginning July 1, 2026) for substitute-teacher costs for the first six weeks of an employee’s FMLA leave ( capped at actual daily costs as determined by the department) and adopt application/disbursement procedures. Covered employees need not use accrued leave for those six weeks. Surpluses (>20% of projected annual needs) transfer by the State Treasurer to an Education Retention Fund for shortages and professional development. The fund is auditable by the Auditor of Public Accounts; misuse triggers repayment and department penalties. Creates the Education Leave and Support Act, designating the State Department of Education ("department") to administer a new State Education Leave Fund and an Education Retention Fund. Beginning Jan 1, 2026, a 0.35% payroll fee on covered teachers' taxable wages is collected by employers (school districts), remitted quarterly to the State Treasurer, and matched dollar-for-dollar by employers. Funds are credited to the State Education Leave Fund, invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment laws, and used solely to reimburse school districts for substitute teacher costs for the first six weeks of a covered employee's FMLA leave (reimbursements begin July 1, 2026). Surpluses over 20% of projected annual needs may be transferred by the State Treasurer to the Education Retention Fund for shortages and professional development. DHHS will set annual fixed-rate reimbursement schedules (effective October 1 each year). Funding: a 0.52% payroll tax (0.39% employer / 0.13% employee) shall fund the program; General Funds are prohibited for costs arising from the income-eligibility changes beginning October 1, 2026. DHHS will administer expanded social services and a child-care subsidy program. Key DHHS duties: contract for services, adopt rules, set an annual fixed rate schedule (effective Oct 1 each year) for child-care reimbursements (cannot exceed providers' private rates; may set separate rates for infants or children with special needs). Effective Oct 1, 2026, DHHS must provide child-care assistance to families with incomes 130%–400% of FPL; ongoing eligibility allows a 10% gross earned income disregard after 12 continuous months and at each redetermination, and assistance is cost-shared on a sliding scale with family contributions capped at transitional child-care rates (as of Jan 1, 2025). 109-1-LB448_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB448_Intro_Copy.docx LB448 (Postconviction Relief Act) expands postconviction relief procedures and identifies the following government actors and fiscal effects:\n\n- District courts: receive and adjudicate verified postconviction motions, may appoint up to two attorneys, order disclosure of prior counsel files, conduct hearings, and enter findings; proceedings are civil.\n- County attorney: must be served notice of postconviction motions.\n- Appellate courts: hear appeals from district court orders; appellate release discretionary.\n- Nebraska Supreme Court and U.S. Supreme Court: referenced as triggers for filing deadlines and retroactive rule application.\n- County boards: required to pay court-fixed fees and expenses to appointed counsel (county-level budgetary obligation).\n\nThe bill creates an actual-innocence claim, time-limit exceptions, and limits the court’s inquiry when excusing procedural defaults. No statewide appropriations are specified. Adds the "Postconviction Relief Act," establishing grounds for relief as constitutional violations or actual innocence. Defines actual innocence standards: newly discovered evidence (e.g., exculpatory DNA, third‑party confessions, impeachment of state witnesses, or forensic scientific evidence undermined by new research) and a clear‑and‑convincing showing that the new evidence likely would have changed the outcome. Defines "applied" and "foundational" validity for forensic methods. Allows district courts to excuse procedural defaults or time limits to prevent manifest injustice if the prisoner makes a colorable actual‑innocence claim; failing to raise ineffective trial‑counsel claims on direct appeal no longer automatically bars them. Permits district courts, on prisoner request, to order prior trial or appellate counsel to produce complete case files. No specific state agencies or departments beyond "district court" and references to "state's" witnesses are named; no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are provided. DOCX | PDF

Counties are prohibited from creating districts that include areas inside a city or village boundary or extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction. Ordinances or county resolutions establishing districts must include findings of public purpose, an assessment‑contract form, an authorized official to execute contracts, an application/eligibility process, assessment collection procedures, and requirements for fixed interest rates and fixed repayment schedules for residential projects. 109-1-LB464_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB464_Intro_Copy.docx LB464 amends criminal statutes (modifying section 28-101, RS Cumulative Supp., 2024) to create and define the offense of organized retail crime, establish related penalties, and repeal the prior version of section 28-101. Key provisions: prior convictions within ten years may be considered; retail market value of losses from a single organized retail crime scheme may be aggregated across victims for offense classification (but not aggregated into more than one offense); aggregate retail market value is an essential element that must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt; and it is not a defense that merchandise was not actually stolen if it was explicitly represented as stolen. No state agencies or departments are named, and no funding or appropriation changes are included. Adds three rules for prosecuting organized retail crime: (1) only conduct within the prior ten years is considered; (2) retail market-value losses from a single organized scheme may be aggregated across victims in one charging instrument to determine offense classification, but may not be aggregated into more than one offense; and (3) aggregate retail market value is an essential element that must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Also clarifies that it is not a defense that merchandise was not actually stolen if it was explicitly represented as stolen, embezzled, or converted. The office will collect, analyze, and publish agencies’ evaluations/duediligence for new rules, enforce analytic standards (e.g., evidence, cost‑benefit, monetized or quantitative estimates where feasible), and may ask agencies and the Governor to reevaluate actions that fail to follow best practices. 109-1-LB477_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB477_Intro_Copy.docx LB477 amends the Workplace Privacy Act to prohibit employers from demanding access to employees’ or applicants’ personal Internet accounts or forcing login, contact-list changes, or settings changes. Exception: the Governor may authorize employer contact tracing during a Governor-declared pandemic state (per §81-829.40) only if the proclamation permits contact tracing, it occurs on employer premises during work hours, and collected data is destroyed within 48 hours after any Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended tracing period. Data that links employees to tracked employer property must be stored by an independent third party and released only by warrant (court/law enforcement). Employers are prohibited from taking adverse actions for refusals or violations. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Original sections are repealed. Added provisions restrict employer-mandated location/tracking apps or wearable devices, except when the Governor issues a pandemic state-of-emergency under section 81-829.40. Under such a proclamation, employers may only perform contact tracing on their premises during work hours; collected data must not be placed in personnel files and must be destroyed within 48 hours after any tracing period recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Employers may track employer-owned property or monitor employer property use so long as data do not associate employees with that property. Any data that does associate an employee must be held by an independent third party and accessed only by warrant. Employers are prohibited from adverse actions based on refusal to comply or on data obtained in violation of the rule. No funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB485_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB485_Intro_Copy.docx LB485 requires that personal identifying information of train crew members appearing in reports and communications concerning railroad fatalities be redacted from public reports and kept confidential by law enforcement and other holders of those records. 109-1-LB487_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB487_Intro_Copy.docx LB487 creates the Restitution and Redress for Redlining Task Force (seven voting members: two appointed from the Commission on African American Affairs and five regionally apportioned by congressional district). The State Treasurer must maintain a newly created Restoration Study Fund (funded by legislative transfers, donations, and transfers from the Marijuana and Controlled Substances Tax Administration Cash Fund) and the state investment officer invests fund balances. The task force may hire staff, subpoena documents, and must terminate November 1, 2028.\n\nFiscal changes: all proceeds of the marijuana/controlled substances tax are credited to the Restoration Study Fund through Nov. 1, 2028. Beginning Nov. 1, 2028, 5% is credited to the Marijuana and Controlled Substances Tax Administration Cash Fund; of the remainder, 50% is remitted to counties for County Drug Law Enforcement and Education Funds and the balance to the Nebraska State Patrol Drug Control and Education Cash Fund. 109-1-LB488_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB488_Intro_Copy.docx LB488 amends probation and juvenile supervision procedures. 109-1-LB48_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB48_Final_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to establish a Family Resource and Juvenile Assessment Center Pilot Program in cities of the metropolitan class (24/7 operation; five-year pilot) and to (1) set a designation process for centers (including self‑assessment and data collection) and (2) conduct annual program evaluations. Funding: designated centers may receive up to $500,000 per center annually from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund; if those funds are unavailable, no General Funds may be used. The Department of Health and Human Services must create a Family Resource and Juvenile Assessment Center Pilot Program in metropolitan-class cities, operating 24/7 and ending five years after the act’s operative date. DHHS will set a designation process requiring centers to meet quality standards, complete a self-assessment (e.g., national Standards of Quality), implement outcome data systems, and provide ongoing post-service supports. The program aims to prevent or reduce juvenile justice involvement through community-based, culturally relevant services. Funding: designated centers may receive up to $500,000 per center annually from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund only; if those funds are unavailable, General Funds cannot be used. 109-1-LB492_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB492_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill amends Nebraska Juvenile Code provisions to explicitly include, in Sec. 2 (amending Neb. Rev. Stat. §43-247), juveniles voluntarily relinquished pursuant to §43-106.01 to the Department of Health and Human Services or to child-placement agencies licensed by the Department as within juvenile-court jurisdiction. The added language tightens the “habitually truant” definition and procedural protections: a child 13–16 is habitually truant only after accruing 20+ unexcused absences with documented educational loss, but a defense exists if, after excluding specified excusable absences, the child has fewer than 20 unexcused days. 109-1-LB493_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB493_Intro_Copy.docx Summary: LB493 adopts the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (an anti‑SLAPP framework), repeals Neb. Rev. Stat. sections 25-21,241 through 25-21,246, and declares an emergency. Key provisions: a defendant may file a special motion to dismiss within 60 days of service; filing generally stays other proceedings; courts must schedule and decide the motion on an expedited timeline (hear within 60 days, rule within 60 days after hearing); standards for dismissal mirror summary‑judgment style review; prevailing moving parties are entitled to court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and litigation expenses; denial of the motion is immediately appealable. No state agencies or departments are named, and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budget allocations. Added provisions set procedures for expedited anti‑SLAPP motions to dismiss under the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act. Key points: courts (the only government entities referenced) must hear such motions within 60 days (with narrow exceptions), filing the motion generally triggers an automatic stay of other proceedings and discovery, and appeals ordinarily stay the action until resolved. Courts may allow limited discovery for specified burdens and may hear emergency public‑health or unrelated motions during a stay. The bill sets standards for dismissal with prejudice, preserves rights after voluntary dismissals, and requires awarding court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and litigation expenses to a prevailing moving party. No executive agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB494_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB494_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services LB494 requires the State Treasurer to transfer $750 million from the General Fund to the School District Property Tax Relief Credit Fund in fiscal year 2024‑25 "on such dates and in such amounts as directed by the budget administrator of the budget division of the Department of Administrative Services." 109-1-LB495_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB495_Intro_Copy.docx LB495 amends the Property Tax Request Act (sections 77-1632 and 77-1633). 109-1-LB496_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB496_Intro_Copy.docx LB496 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60-6,111 (Nebraska Rules of the Road) to clarify duties when animals are on roadways. Riders/drivers of animals, animal‑drawn vehicles, farm tractors, and implements of husbandry retain vehicle‑driver rights and duties and, when obstructing traffic, must move to the nearest shoulder. New subsection defines livestock (horse, mule, donkey, cattle, swine, sheep, goat) and imposes specific obligations on motorists: exercise caution when approaching or passing livestock handlers, stop promptly if a handler gives a distress signal (unless stopping would cause an accident), turn off the engine if requested, and yield right of way to livestock. The bill repeals the original section. No agencies, appropriations, or budget changes are referenced. Adds a new subsection defining "livestock" (horse, mule, donkey, cattle, swine, sheep, goat) and requires motorists on highways to: (1) use caution when approaching or passing anyone leading/herding livestock; (2) stop if the person leading/driving livestock gives a distress signal by raising a hand (unless moving is necessary to avoid an accident); (3) turn off the vehicle engine if requested by that person; and (4) yield right of way to livestock being led/driven. No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations are referenced or changed. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB497_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB497_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB497 amends section 79-215 to address residency and payment rules where the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) is involved. 109-1-LB498_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB498_Intro_Copy.docx LB498 amends the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act. It directs the Department (state education agency) to calculate foundation aid: $1,500 per formula student for 2023-24 and 2024-25, and beginning 2025-26 a per‑student amount indexed annually to the prior calendar year's CPI‑U. Twenty‑four percent of total foundation aid is to be paid from the Education Future Fund. For 2023-24/24-25 all foundation aid is a formula resource; for 2025-26 onward 60% is a formula resource.\n\nThe Department must certify aid, district budget authority, and applicable reserve percentages to the Director of Administrative Services, Auditor of Public Accounts, and local systems on or before June 15, 2025, and March 1 annually thereafter, and report funding needs to the Governor, Appropriations Committee, and Education Committee. Prior certifications for 2025‑26 are void. The Appropriations Committee must include the necessary state aid amount in its budget recommendations. Emergency clause makes the act effective on enactment. Adds an annual CPI-based index to foundation aid starting in school year 2025‑26. For 2025‑26 and each year after, each district’s foundation aid = (prior year’s foundation aid paid per formula student, increased by the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers as published by the Federal Bureau of Labor Statistics for the previous calendar year) × (the district’s number of formula students). The provision references school years 2023‑24 and 2024‑25 but gives the CPI indexing effective 2025‑26. No specific dollar appropriations or budget line items are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB4_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB4_Intro_Copy.docx LB4 (2025) amends PSC jurisdiction and adopts the Telecommunications Exchange Deregulation Act. It explicitly places the Act under the Nebraska Public Service Commission's authority, authorizing the PSC to require carrier disclosures, protect claimed proprietary information per section 84-712.05, and adopt rules to administer, deregulate, reregulate, or review exchanges. Only an electing local exchange carrier may petition to deregulate an exchange; the PSC must decide within 90 days using census-based population or multi-carrier presence tests (including an alternative 75% coverage test). Deregulated carriers are relieved of carrier-of-last-resort, service-quality reporting, and most pricing obligations. Transitioning carriers lose eligibility for Nebraska Telecommunications Universal Service Fund support for deregulated exchanges, and the PSC must reduce fund allocations accordingly. The bill revises related statutory cross-references and repeals the original sections. Key agency actions and funding changes:\n\n- "The commission" (the state telecommunications regulator) may require carrier disclosures, protect proprietary submissions under section 84-712.05, adopt rules, and must decide deregulation petitions within 90 days. \n- The commission will use U.S. Bureau of the Census decennial or revised counts to determine exchange populations and must reclassify carriers following deregulation. \n- Deregulated carriers are relieved of carrier-of-last-resort, service-quality reporting, and most pricing obligations (except pricing conditions tied to grants administered by the commission). \n- Transitioning carriers lose eligibility for the Nebraska Telecommunications Universal Service Fund for deregulated exchanges; the commission shall, to the extent feasible in the funding formula, reduce their fund allocations. \n- Discontinuance procedures for service in deregulated exchanges are narrowed to subsection (1)(b) of section 86-134. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB500_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB500_Intro_Copy.docx Creates a 21-member School Financing Review Commission with members drawn from state agencies and bodies: Commissioner of Education (or designee), a Governor appointee, three nonvoting legislative members (including members of the Education and Revenue Committees), the Property Tax Administrator (or designee), a postsecondary education representative, an Educational Service Unit Coordinating Council member, multiple school board members and administrators representing Class III–V districts, a certificated teacher, and six at-large members. The commission must submit a final report to the Governor, State Board of Education, and Legislature by December 1, 2025; thereafter it will review state education missions/goals, solicit stakeholder input, assess implementation of the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act, and file biennial adequacy reports by July 1 of even years 2028–2034. Bill takes effect on enactment. No budgetary appropriations or funding changes are included. Creates a 21‑member School Financing Review Commission. Members include the Commissioner of Education (or designee), the Property Tax Administrator (or designee), one Governor appointee, three nonvoting legislators, a postsecondary school‑finance expert, an Educational Service Unit Coordinating Council member, multiple school board members and administrators from Class III–V districts, a certificated teacher, and six at‑large members (two per congressional district). The commission must deliver a final report to the Governor, the State Board of Education, and the Legislature by December 1, 2025, and then report biennially on school funding adequacy (by July 1 of even years 2028–2034). It will review the State Department of Education’s mission, recommend goals/best practices, and review implementation of the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB501_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB501_Final_Copy.docx LB501 amends statutes governing assessment and post-damage valuation procedures, reallocating duties and timelines among local and state tax authorities. Key agencies/departments affected:\n- County assessors: must inspect reported damaged property and submit a prescribed report to the county board of equalization by July 20; preliminary valuation notice timing retained for large counties.\n- County clerks: receive owner damage reports (due by July 15) on Tax Commissioner forms.\n- County boards of equalization: must adjust assessments to the value on the damage date, may meet June 1–July 25 (or through Aug 10 with an extension), and handle notices/protests and appeals to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission.\n- County treasurers: collection/enforcement duties (distress warrants) do not apply to property classified as damaged.\n- Tax Commissioner: prescribes reporting forms.\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. The bill repeals prior sections and takes effect immediately as an emergency measure. Adds a requirement that the county assessor inspect and review all properties for which a report is filed under this section and submit a comprehensive report to the county board of equalization by July 20 of the current assessment year. The report must use a form prescribed by the Tax Commissioner and include all property-owner reports filed under this section. Agencies mentioned: county assessor, county board of equalization, and the Tax Commissioner. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB502_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB502_Intro_Copy.docx LB502 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §48-1714 (Farm Labor Contractors Act) to specify criminal penalties: violations of §48-1711 or §48-1712 are Class II misdemeanors; intentionally defacing/altering or misusing a farm labor contractor license, permitting such use, or acting without a license are Class II misdemeanors; and seed corn producers or farm labor contractors who violate §48-1715 are guilty of a Class IV misdemeanor. The bill repeals the original §48-1714 and states it harmonizes provisions. No state agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. Adds a criminal penalty: any seed corn producer or farm labor contractor who violates §48-1715 commits a Class IV misdemeanor. No government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB503_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB503_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue The bill defines "Department" as the Department of Revenue and assigns these specific responsibilities to it:\n\n- Receive and process county applications for "American energy friendly" designation on a department-prescribed form; designate qualifying counties within 30 days and notify the county board; maintain a current list on its website of applicants/designated counties. \n- Collect and enforce the nameplate capacity tax (including a referenced tax rate), require annual owner reports (filed March 1), and prorate tax changes when a county gains or loses designation. \n- Separately identify tax proceeds from this section and remit them to the county treasurer where the facility is located within 30 days of receipt. \n- Adopt and promulgate rules and regulations necessary to implement the section.\n\nNo direct changes to department appropriations or other state budget appropriations are provided in the bill text. Key provisions affecting the Department of Revenue (the "department"):\n- "Department" is defined as the Department of Revenue.\n- The department must accept county applications (on a department-prescribed form) and, if statutory conditions are met, designate a county as an "American energy friendly county" and notify the county board within 30 days of receipt.\n- The department must maintain a current list on its website of counties that have applied/been designated.\n- The department may adopt rules and regulations to implement the section.\n- The department is tied to tax administration: the increased nameplate-capacity tax for owners of privately developed renewable facilities is prorated in the first year a county gains or loses the designation (based on days designated).\n\nNo new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the department are specified. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB504_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB504_Final_Copy.docx LB504 (2025) enacts the Age-Appropriate Online Design Code Act. Key government entities referenced:\n\n- Attorney General: Enforcement authority for violations (also treated as deceptive trade practices). The AG may not seek civil penalties under the Act until July 1, 2026. Beginning July 1, 2026, covered services may face civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation.\n\n- State Treasurer: All penalties collected must be remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution pursuant to Article VII, §5 of the Nebraska Constitution.\n\nFederal agencies cited for definitions/standards include the Federal Trade Commission (dark patterns) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPI adjustments); federal health and privacy laws/agencies (HITECH, HIPAA, FDA-related human subject protections) are noted as exceptions. The Act becomes operative January 1, 2026. Adds an Age-Appropriate Online Design Code with multiple federal and state agency references and limited fiscal actions. Key agencies mentioned: Federal Bureau of Labor Statistics (CPI used to adjust a $25M revenue threshold), Federal Trade Commission (FTC) — including FTC definitions of “dark pattern” and COPPA/FTC rules, Attorney General (enforcement; cannot seek civil penalties until July 1, 2026), State Treasurer (all collected civil penalties remitted for distribution per Neb. Const. Art. VII, §5), Health & Human Services–related federal statutes/regulators via references to GLBA (Title V), HITECH, HIPAA (section 264 regs), and the Food and Drug Administration and International Council for Harmonisation for clinical-trial exemptions. Fiscal provisions: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation; no new appropriations or budget line-items are created—penalties are remitted to the State Treasurer for constitutional distribution. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB505_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB505_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture, Department of Health and Human Services LB505 directs intent to appropriate $10,000,000 for FY2025‑26 and $10,000,000 for FY2026‑27 from federal funds to the Department of Health and Human Services, Program No. 347 (Public Assistance). The funding is specified as federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funds for grants to nonprofit organizations that provide food assistance, operate in ten or more Nebraska counties, and qualify for the Emergency Food Assistance Program administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The bill contains an emergency clause making it effective upon passage. - Department of Health and Human Services: Intends to appropriate $10,000,000 in FY2025-26 and $10,000,000 in FY2026-27 (Federal Funds) to Program No. 347, Public Assistance. Funds are from the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program and allocated as grants to nonprofit organizations that (1) provide food assistance, (2) distribute food in ten or more Nebraska counties, and (3) qualify for the USDA Emergency Food Assistance Program.\n\n- Department of Agriculture: No direct state funding or appropriation changes. The bill requires grantees to be eligible for the federal USDA Emergency Food Assistance Program, which is federally administered. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB506_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB506_Intro_Copy.docx LB506 (Landlord and Tenant Radon Awareness Act) requires lessors — a term that expressly includes government agencies and subdivisions — to provide prospective tenants (at application) and tenants (on request) with a radon-hazard disclosure and any available radon test results. Radon measurement and mitigation specialists must be licensed under the Radiation Control Act; lessors must provide test results to tenants within ten days of receipt. The bill prohibits withholding a tenant’s security deposit for radon testing or mitigation, except where a tenant installed an unapproved mitigation system that was not properly installed by a licensed radon mitigation specialist. Applies to leases executed on or after the act’s effective date. No funding or appropriation changes. Adds the "Landlord and Tenant Radon Awareness Act," requiring lessors to provide radon information and a standardized disclosure to prospective and current tenants, and prohibiting retention of security deposits for radon testing/mitigation except for improperly installed tenant‑installed systems. It defines key terms (dwelling unit, lease, lessor, tenant, mitigation, radon hazard) and specifies that "radon measurement specialist" and "radon mitigation specialist" must be licensed under the Radiation Control Act. "Lessor" explicitly includes government agencies or subdivisions. The bill references the State of Nebraska's recommendation for testing. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB507_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB507_Intro_Copy.docx LB507 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79‑1129 to clarify transportation and service obligations for children with disabilities. Resident school boards must provide transportation or transportation expenses when children must leave the district for services or require special transportation, reimbursing parents/guardians at the mileage rate in §81‑1176 for actual miles traveled (payment limited to one child when multiple disabled children are transported; no payment for untraveled mileage). The bill also requires provision of visiting teachers for homebound students, correspondence instruction, or other methods approved by the Commissioner of Education. Nonresident school districts may, by mutual agreement with the district of residence, provide transportation expenses. The original §79‑1129 is repealed. No new appropriations or specific budget allocations are included. Adds the phrase "enrolled in the school district," narrowing applicability to individuals officially enrolled in that district. No government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB508_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB508_Intro_Copy.docx LB508 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §55-117 (Military Code). It: (1) bars the Nebraska National Guard from being ordered into active combat under federal service unless the U.S. Congress has declared war or has "called forth" the Guard pursuant to the U.S. Constitution to enforce federal law, suppress insurrection, or repel invasions; (2) requires the Governor to review all current federal orders placing Guard members into active combat for compliance with that restriction and to take any actions necessary to immediately return noncompliant members to Nebraska; (3) requires the Governor to report the review and any actions to the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee within 30 days after completion; (4) defines "active combat;" and (5) preserves the Governor’s control through the Adjutant General (with local police subject to that control when Guard is ordered). No funding or appropriation changes. Section 55-118 is repealed. Adds that the Nebraska National Guard may not be ordered into active combat unless Congress has declared war or otherwise called the Guard under the U.S. Constitution. Requires the Governor to review all current federal orders that placed Guard members into active combat for compliance; if an order is noncompliant the Governor must take action to immediately return those members to Nebraska. The Governor must report the review and any actions to the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee within 30 days of completing the review. Defines “active combat” by three criteria. No agencies receive new funding and no appropriations or budget changes are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB509_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB509_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue The bill defines "Department" as the Department of Revenue and assigns it key administrative duties for the Opportunity Scholarships Act. The Department must certify (and may revoke certification of) scholarship‑granting organizations that meet statutory criteria. Scholarship organizations must notify the Department of each taxpayer's intended tax‑credit amount; the Department has 30 days to determine availability and must process notifications in receipt order. The Department also tracks whether contributions are received within required timeframes and excludes untimely amounts when enforcing the program's annual tax‑credit cap. The annual cap is $25 million for 2025–2027 and thereafter adjusts annually (up to $100 million) per the bill. No direct appropriations or budget allocations are specified. The act is operative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. Department of Revenue duties and fiscal effects:\n- The department is defined as the Department of Revenue and must certify and may revoke certification of scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) meeting 501(c)(3) and program requirements (priority rules, scholarship limits, average award cap of 75% of statewide per‑student spending).\n- Administrative role: SGOs notify the department of taxpayers' intended credit amounts; the department must determine within 30 days if amounts exceed the annual cap and notify the SGO. Notifications are processed in receipt order.\n- Fiscal/credit rules the department administers: nonrefundable income tax credits (carryforward 5 years) with taxpayer caps (generally lesser of contribution, 50% of tax liability, or $100,000; estates/trusts $1,000,000). Taxpayers may not direct scholarships to specific students.\n- Annual statewide credit cap: $25 million for 2025–2027, then may grow (125% if prior year usage >90%, otherwise unchanged) up to a $100 million ceiling. No direct appropriations to the department are specified; credits will reduce state revenue within those caps. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB50_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB50_Final_Copy.docx Department of Revenue The bill amends §77-6204 so that county treasurers must distribute all revenue received from the Department of Revenue under §77-6203 (5% to the community college area where the facility is located; the remainder to eligible local taxing entities). It also expressly prohibits the Department of Revenue from retaining any revenue collected under §§77-6201–77-6204 for distribution, use, transfer, pledge, or allocation to or from the General Fund. No other changes to Department of Revenue appropriations or budget line-item funding are included. Adds a revenue distribution rule for receipts tied to renewable energy generation facilities: the Department of Revenue must allocate 5% of that revenue to the community college area where the facility is located; the remaining 95% is to be distributed according to existing subdivision (1)(b). No new appropriations or agency budget increases are specified — the change only reallocates the distribution percentages DOR must apply. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB510_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB510_Intro_Copy.docx LB510 amends sales-tax and Good Life district administration. It assigns the Department (Revenue) authority to approve applications, adjust boundaries, accept evidence of investment commitments, transmit application/approval materials to affected cities/villages (subject to confidentiality), and terminate districts only if investment commitments miss 10%/50%/75% thresholds at years 3/7/10. The bill conditions the post‑July 1, 2025 reduced state sales-tax rate within Good Life districts to apply only on portions inside a city/village corporate limit and only after that city/village has imposed a local sales or occupation tax of at least 2.75%. Cities must obtain voter approval to appropriate local revenue (including local option sales/use and occupation taxes) to Good Life district programs and file election resolutions with election commissioners/county clerks per statutory deadlines. Nebraska State Fair Board and public ownership exceptions remain; the act takes effect immediately. - Commencing July 1, 2025 the state sales tax rate (section 77-2703) becomes 5.5%, but transactions inside the portion of a Good Life district located within a city or village are taxed at 2.75%—only if that city or village has imposed at least a 2.75% local sales or occupation tax on those transactions. \n- On and after July 1, 2025 transactions in a Good Life district are subject to the reduced state rate referenced in subdivision (7) of section 77-2701.02. \n- "The department" (the administering state department for the Good Life Acts) must accept evidence from property owners or cities/villages and may treat such owner(s) or city/village as the Good Life district applicant for all statutory purposes, and may not terminate a Good Life district until at least three years after establishment. \n- Cities/villages may not use eminent domain to acquire district property for transfer or sale to private parties. \n- No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified beyond the tax-rate changes. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB511_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB511_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Motor Vehicles The bill requires the Department of Correctional Services to provide written notice of sex‑offender registration duties to anyone committed for a registrable offense prior to release; the individual must read and sign the form, which the department retains and forwards (with a copy to the person) to the Nebraska State Patrol. The Department of Motor Vehicles must be queried when seized property is a Nebraska‑titled motor vehicle and must seek out‑of‑state title/licensing records when applicable; DMV license and commercial driver’s license applications must include written notice of registration duties. The Department of Health and Human Services must run education/outreach on healthy families, pornography, and prostitution, include DHHS‑employee assaults as predicate offenses under the Public Protection Act, and hold affiliation agreements with nonprofit victim service providers under the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act. Legislative intent appropriates $100,000 (FY2025‑26) to the Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice for grants and $25,000 (FY2025‑26) to the Nebraska State Patrol to implement registration changes. - Department of Correctional Services: New duties require DCS (or city/county jails) to have persons subject to sex‑offender registration read and sign a written notification of the duty to register, retain a signed copy, and provide copies to the individual and to the Sex Offender Registration & Community Notification Division of the Nebraska State Patrol.\n\n- Department of Health and Human Services: No substantive additions, duties, or budget changes affecting DHHS are included in the added text.\n\n- Department of Motor Vehicles: No substantive additions, duties, or budget changes affecting the DMV are included in the added text.\n\n- Funding/appropriations: The bill expresses legislative intent to appropriate $100,000 (FY2025‑26) to the Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement & Criminal Justice for enforcement grants, and $25,000 (FY2025‑26) to the Nebraska State Patrol for registration implementation; no direct appropriations to DCS, DHHS, or DMV. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB512_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB512_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill defines "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services and assigns it specific duties under the Chemical Abortion Safety Protocol Act. Physicians must file monthly reports with the department within 30 days after the end of the calendar month in which an abortion‑inducing drug was provided; reports must include specified non‑identifying data and any additional information required by rules and regulations the department adopts. The department must produce a standard form for these reports. The bill contains no provisions for funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. Adds the "Chemical Abortion Safety Protocol Act," defining terms (including "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services) and imposing clinical, documentation, follow‑up, and reporting duties on physicians who provide abortion‑inducing drugs. DHHS duties: produce a standard reporting form and receive physician reports (filed within 30 days after the end of the calendar month of provision) that must include physician name, drug(s) and dates, follow‑up date, adverse events, treatments, and referrals; reports must exclude personally identifying patient information. The department may adopt rules prescribing additional report content. No appropriations, new funding, or budget allocations for DHHS are specified in the added text. DOCX | PDF
