109-1-LB513_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB513_Final_Copy.docx LB513 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §24-201.01 to adjust compensation for the Chief Justice and justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court. Salaries are set at $228,431.18 effective July 1, 2025, and $231,857.65 effective July 1, 2026 (prior salary on July 1, 2024 was $225,055.35). Salaries remain payable in equal monthly installments and judges are prohibited from holding other paid public offices. The bill repeals the original section, states an operative date of July 1, 2025, and includes an emergency clause so it takes effect upon passage and approval. No separate appropriations or explicit budget allocations are included in the text; these increases will raise state compensation expenditures for the Nebraska Supreme Court. Adds scheduled salary increases for the State Supreme Court: effective July 1, 2025 the Chief Justice and justices’ annual salary is set at $228,431.18; effective July 1, 2026 it is set at $231,857.65. Affects the Supreme Court judiciary compensation; the provision itself does not specify funding sources, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB514_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB514_Intro_Copy.docx LB514 (Urban Affairs Committee) amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §14-102 to authorize cities of the metropolitan class to regulate local housing authorities. New expressly enumerated powers allow such cities to require code enforcement and pest control for housing authority‑owned/controlled properties; mandate regular inspections; require registration under local rental‑registration ordinances; set penalties for code and management failures; and require monthly updates to the city council. The bill repeals the original §14-102. No state agency appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations are included. Adds authority for a city of the metropolitan class to regulate its housing authority. Permissible measures include requiring city code enforcement and pest control for housing authority‑owned properties; regular inspections of managed properties; registration of those properties under the city’s rental registration ordinance; penalties for code violations or mismanagement; and monthly reports/updates to the city council. No state agencies, new departments, or changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB515_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB515_Intro_Copy.docx LB515 (Health and Human Services Committee) amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §38-28,104 (Pharmacy Practice Act). It authorizes a pharmacist (or a practitioner with a pharmacy license under §38-2850) to dispense an emergency refill of up to a 30‑day supply—or the amount of the most recent refill, whichever is less—when refill authorization cannot be readily obtained, provided: the drug is noncontrolled, is a maintenance medication, the pharmacist documents prescription information from a label, any pharmacy record, or a common database, and the pharmacist judges interruption of therapy would harm the patient. Controlled substances remain subject to §§28-414 and 28-414.01. The bill repeals the original section. No state agency funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds authority for pharmacists, when unable to obtain refill authorization, to dispense an emergency refill of up to a 30‑day supply (or the amount of the most recent refill, whichever is less) if: they obtain prescription information from a label, any pharmacy record, or a common database; the drug is not a controlled substance; it is a maintenance medication; and in the pharmacist’s professional judgment interruption of therapy would harm the patient. No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations are mentioned or changed. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB516_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB516_Intro_Copy.docx LB516 repeals sections 68-130 and 81-1139.01, R.R.S., removes an existing statutory requirement that counties provide office space related to the Department of Health and Human Services, and eliminates related obsolete provisions. No changes to funding, appropriations, or departmental budgets are included. No underlined (added) text found in this bill. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB517_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB517_Intro_Copy.docx LB517 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79-2,144 to expand and detail duties of the state school security director (within the State Department of Education). Key provisions require each school district to provide the director with safety and security plans plus annual inspection information for protective door assemblies, door-locking systems, and double-entry doors, and any other security information requested (submissions may be withheld under the public records exemption in §84-712.05). The director must establish standards for protective door assemblies and require annual inspections by trained inspectors, continue security assessments and training programs, recommend minimum standards to the State Board of Education, and carry out the department’s obligations under the School Safety and Security Reporting System Act. The bill repeals the original section. No funding, appropriation, or budget changes are specified. Adds standards requiring school boards to ensure annual inspections of protective door assemblies in school buildings by trained inspectors with relevant door-assembly and building-security expertise. Specifies that “protective door assemblies” include: doors with panic or fire-exit hardware; door assemblies in exit enclosures; electronically controlled egress doors; and doors with special locking arrangements (e.g., delayed egress, sensor-released egress, elevator‑lobby doors). No state agencies beyond local school districts/boards are named, and no funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB518_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB518_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services LB518 amends §83‑1,100.03 to require the Department of Correctional Services (department), in consultation with the Board of Parole, to help adopt rules to reduce inmates who serve full sentences and are released without supervision. Rules must ensure parolees receive at least nine months of supervision, prioritize meaningful transition periods, and require that each parole-eligible inmate be assessed with a validated risk-and-needs assessment provided by the department; assessed risk, criminal history, program completion, institutional conduct, and other individual factors must inform release decisions. Annually by February 1, the department and board must electronically report to the Legislature, Supreme Court, and Governor on percentages and characteristics of inmates released without supervision and provide policy/practice recommendations. No appropriations or funding changes are included. The added text requires the report to be submitted electronically and to include three enumerated components: (a) "Describe," (b) "Document," and (c) "Provide." The excerpt supplies no substance for those items. There are no references to the Department of Correctional Services, nor any language altering funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. As written, the addition imposes a reporting format requirement but creates no identifiable fiscal or operational changes for the Department of Correctional Services. If the omitted content for (a)–(c) is later specified, fiscal impacts should be reassessed. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB519_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB519_Final_Copy.docx LB519 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §83-4,114.02 (correctional services) to require the department to provide independent confirmatory testing before taking disciplinary action for drug or alcohol violations. The requirement is expanded from urinalysis to include any screening, field, presumptive, or spot test of items suspected of being or containing contraband drugs. If the confirmatory test remains positive, the inmate must pay the cost of that test. The bill repeals the original section. No statewide appropriations or agency budget increases are specified; the cost responsibility is shifted to inmates when confirmatory tests remain positive. Adds definitions clarifying that covered drug testing includes (1)(a) urinalysis and (1)(b) any screening, field, presumptive, or spot test of an item suspected of containing contraband drugs. No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations are referenced or changed. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB51_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB51_Final_Copy.docx LB51 ratifies the National Crime Prevention and Privacy Compact (34 U.S.C. §40316) to enable authorized interstate exchange of criminal history record information for noncriminal justice purposes. The Superintendent of Law Enforcement and Public Safety is directed to execute the compact and, as compact officer (or by designee), to administer it for Nebraska. The Nebraska State Patrol is designated as the state repository for criminal history records, authorized to take necessary actions and to adopt rules, regulations, and procedures for cooperative exchanges with federal authorities. Ratification remains until expressly renounced by statute. The bill preserves existing Nebraska obligations (including the Security, Privacy, and Dissemination of Criminal History Information Act) and does not change public access provisions. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. The bill ratifies Nebraska’s participation in the National Crime Prevention and Privacy Compact (34 U.S.C. 40316). It directs the Superintendent of Law Enforcement and Public Safety to execute the compact and to serve (or designate) as the state’s compact officer. The Nebraska State Patrol is named the state repository for criminal history record information for compact purposes, authorized to carry out the compact, adopt rules and procedures, and coordinate exchanges with the federal government for noncriminal-justice uses. Ratification remains until the Legislature enacts a law renouncing the compact. The compact explicitly does not alter the Nebraska State Patrol’s existing state-law duties (including the Security, Privacy, and Dissemination of Criminal History Information Act) or public access to criminal history records. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB520_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB520_Intro_Copy.docx LB520 amends statutes governing bed and breakfast (B&B) establishments. It requires the State Fire Marshal to incorporate B&B-specific provisions into the State Fire Code, to enforce the Code via inspections, compliance orders, and plan review, and to assess a $50 penalty for plans submitted after construction in addition to the existing plan review fee (per section 81-505.01). The bill also requires the unnamed "department" referenced in the Nebraska Pure Food Act to offer a food-handler certification examination for B&B operators. New safety requirements to be enforced under the Fire Code include smoke alarms and heat detectors, emergency egress lighting, a smoking ban, primary and secondary egress or sprinklers (with an 18-month compliance window), minimum fire extinguisher ratings by floor and kitchen, and hood fire suppression for kitchens serving hot meals to more than ten guests. No appropriations or budget changes are included. Adds detailed food-safety and fire/safety requirements for bed-and-breakfasts and assigns limited oversight to "the department" (unspecified in the text) to: approve thawing methods and offer the food-handler certification exam operators must pass. Food rules include storage, temperature controls, use of pasteurized Grade A milk, limited home-canned goods, hygiene and exclusion of communicable-foodborne workers, utensil/sanitation rules, and required indicating thermometers. Fire/safety rules require smoke alarms, heat detectors, emergency lighting, indoor smoking prohibition, primary and secondary egress (with sprinkler-system exemptions), an 18‑month compliance period to add egress or sprinklers, specified fire-extinguisher ratings per floor/kitchen, and a fire-suppression hood for kitchens that serve hot meals and host over ten guests. 109-1-LB521_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB521_Final_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services, Department of Motor Vehicles The bill requires the Department of Motor Vehicles to: enter an agreement with the Secretary of State to match DMV records (including citizenship verification) against the statewide voter registration list; enter an agreement with the Social Security Administration; provide voter registration applications at issuance/renewal of operator licenses and state ID cards; electronically transmit registration data and provide digital images/signatures to county election officials within prescribed timeframes; and allow DMV-provided information to trigger cancellation of a Nebraska registration when a license/ID is surrendered to another state. 109-1-LB522_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB522_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Labor The bill adds annual cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) to long-term weekly workers’ compensation benefits beginning in 2026. The COLA percentage is defined as the greater of 1% or "the percentage change, for the most recent twelve‑month period for which information is available, in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, as prepared by the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics." No changes to Department of Labor funding, appropriations, or other budget allocations are included. Beginning Jan. 1, 2026, weekly workers’ compensation income benefits that continue beyond 12 months will receive automatic annual COLAs. COLA = the greater of 1% or the most recent 12‑month change in the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. Dept. of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics). The Nebraska Workers’ Compensation Court will set the annual COLA each Jan. 1. Adjustments occur at each 12‑month anniversary, are rounded up to the next whole dollar, and are capped by the applicable statutory maximum weekly benefit (sections 48‑121.01 and 48‑122). For benefits under section 48‑122, the limitation in 48‑122.03 does not restrict COLA increases. No departmental funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB52_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB52_Final_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services The bill amends victim-notification duties for the Department of Correctional Services (DCS) and the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). DCS and DHHS must include victim names in offender files (not public) and accept written victim requests for notification while offenders are under their jurisdiction (with a three‑year post‑jurisdiction request window when DHHS is involved). DCS must notify victims of furloughs/releases (≥24 hours), transfers to community status, community‑based program placements/terminations, escapes/returns, discharges, earliest release/parole calculations, sentence reductions, and victims’ right to submit statements. When commitment petitions are filed, DCS forwards victim names to DHHS; DHHS must notify victims of petitions, escapes/returns, discharge/changes in disposition, furloughs/releases (≥24 hours), and program placements/terminations. DCS and DHHS must adopt implementing rules. Victim contact information held by DCS and DHHS is exempt from public disclosure. No funding or appropriation changes are included. Added language expands the statutory list of enumerated offenses to include multiple violent and sexual crimes—e.g., manslaughter; motor vehicle homicide; first- and second-degree assault; assault by strangulation/suffocation; terroristic threats; stalking; false imprisonment in the first degree; sexual offenses including sexual abuse by a school employee, sexual assault of a child, sexual abuse of a protected individual; child enticement via electronic communication device; domestic assault (1st/2nd); and sex/labor trafficking (including minors).\n\nImpacts: Department of Correctional Services may see increased caseloads, incarceration and supervision needs tied to these offenses. Department of Health and Human Services may face greater demand for victim services, child protection, mental‑health and treatment programs. 109-1-LB539_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB539_Intro_Copy.docx LB539 amends Nebraska handgun statutes by narrowing and harmonizing criminal-history check procedures and revising who receives what information. The Nebraska State Patrol is limited to receiving only the information necessary to determine eligibility (including concealed‑carry permit qualifications) and must provide chiefs of police or sheriffs only whether an applicant is disqualified from purchasing or possessing a handgun. The bill preserves immunity for persons, agencies, or mental‑health boards that report records in good faith and creates a Class II misdemeanor for knowingly causing the Patrol to request checks without reasonable belief of an application. Licensed federal importers, manufacturers, and dealers must inspect a valid certificate and photo identification before transfer; knowingly falsifying information in a handgun purchase/transfer is a Class IV felony. The bill repeals numerous related statutory sections. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds that criminal-history record checks for firearms or explosives include persons qualified for a concealed-carry permit under statute 69-2430 or anyone otherwise required to undergo such a check by law/this section. 109-1-LB53_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB53_Intro_Copy.docx LB53 declares the Legislature’s intent not to criminalize pregnancy or punish pregnancy outcomes and establishes both criminal and civil immunity for individuals regarding their own pregnancy outcomes. 109-1-LB540_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB540_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture LB540 amends the Nebraska Apiary Act to expressly define "Department" as the Department of Agriculture and "Director" as the Director of Agriculture (or designated representative). 109-1-LB541_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB541_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services, Department of Motor Vehicles The bill requires the Secretary of State to contract with the Department of Administrative Services (DAS) to store and distribute official election forms. The DMV must provide voter registration applications at license/ID offices, permit electronic transmission of registration data (including digital image and signature) to county election officials, and assist verification of driver’s license/ID data for mailed‑ballot requests. The Secretary of State will supply DMV with voter‑ID outreach materials. Proceeds from sale of official registration applications are remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Election Administration Fund. No other bill sections reference or appropriate funds for DAS or DMV. The added provisions tighten election procedures—defining “hand count,” limiting it to voter‑marked paper ballots (including ballots marked by assistive machines), requiring covert‑watermark and signature verification, mandating secure ballot drop‑box standards (marking, lighting, tamper resistance, 24/7 video, pre‑election inspections, repair deadlines, public release of recordings within five days, 22‑month retention), requiring deputy registrars and early‑ballot applicants to present valid photographic ID, limiting employer agents, and providing for hand‑count audits (at least 25% and recount options). 109-1-LB543_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB543_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles LB543 authorizes the Department (Motor Vehicles) to deliver license plates and registration certificates by secure mail or alternative shipping, with an implementation date to be set by the director on or before January 1, 2029. The bill permits multiyear (two- or three-year) registrations (implementation by director by Jan. 1, 2029). 109-1-LB546_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB546_Intro_Copy.docx LB546 amends §81-829.40 to reaffirm and clarify the Governor’s authority over emergency management and the Nebraska Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), including general direction and control of NEMA and emergency management functions. 109-1-LB548_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB548_Intro_Copy.docx LB548 permits a political subdivision (e.g., a municipality) that owns and operates a natural gas system to contract to sell natural gas to an industrial consumer located in Nebraska that requires at least 3 billion Btu per day on an average day. 109-1-LB549_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB549_Intro_Copy.docx LB549 authorizes school boards to employ chaplains (including volunteers) to provide academic, career, emotional, and behavioral supports without holding a state teaching or administrative certificate. 109-1-LB550_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB550_Intro_Copy.docx LB550 requires Nebraska school districts to adopt a policy excusing students to attend released‑time courses for religious instruction if parental consent and district conditions are met. Key district obligations: treat excused students as attending for purposes of school funding and attendance requirements; permit academic credit only after secular evaluation using the same criteria as similar courses; restrict released‑time instruction from district property unless allowed under an equal‑access policy that opens facilities to community groups; and not deny released‑time sponsors equal access to funds, benefits, or services available to community groups. The bill authorizes civil actions against school districts for violations (actual damages, equitable/declaratory relief, and attorney’s fees). The act takes effect immediately under an emergency clause. Adds rules for "released time" courses: students excused to attend such courses are counted as attending their school for purposes of school funding and attendance. School districts may grant academic credit using secular, neutral criteria and must not base credit decisions on religious content. Released time programs and sponsors get equal access to any funds, benefits, or services the school district makes available to community groups. Enforcement allows aggrieved persons/organizations to sue the school district for actual damages, equitable relief, and reasonable attorney fees. No specific new appropriations or agency budget allocations are created; the change affects how student attendance is counted for school funding. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB551_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB551_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services LB551 requires community college areas to file two annual audits with the Department of Administrative Services (in addition to the Auditor of Public Accounts and the Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education): (1) a comprehensive audit of books, accounts, records and affairs covering the most recently completed fiscal year, including all revenue sources used for operations and capital improvements and the county‑certified property valuation—filed by November 15; and (2) a comprehensive audit of full‑time equivalent student enrollment and reimbursable educational unit totals for the most recently completed fiscal year, including a three‑year verified report used for aid calculations—filed by August 15. The bill contains no explicit changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. The added provisions prohibit the Board of Regents, the Board of Trustees of the Nebraska State Colleges, and community college boards from creating or authorizing any new academic tenure system for employees who are not already tenured as of the act’s effective date. Each board must adopt written policies covering employee agreements; acceptable grounds for dismissal (explicitly including just cause, program discontinuance, and financial exigency); annual faculty performance evaluations; minimum standards of faculty practice; standards for review and discipline; and procedures for dismissal for just cause, program discontinuance, and financial exigency. 109-1-LB552_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB552_Intro_Copy.docx LB552 prohibits public postsecondary institutions in Nebraska—those governed by the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska, the Board of Trustees of the Nebraska State Colleges, and community college governing boards—from maintaining a "diversity, equity, and inclusion" (DEI) office or implementing DEI actions that influence hiring, provide preferential treatment, adopt race-/gender‑referenced policies, require employee participation in DEI programs, or use public funds for DEI programs or offices. Exceptions include sexual‑harassment training; offices of licensed attorneys for legal compliance; statements required for grants/accreditation (e.g., support for first‑generation, low‑income, underserved students or compliance certifications); certain data collection, research, student organization activities, and short‑term speakers. Employees may sue institutions for violations and seek injunctive relief. No specific appropriations or new funding are provided; the bill bars public spending on DEI programs/offices. Adds definitions tying implementation to the appropriate governing boards: the Board of Regents (University of Nebraska), the Board of Trustees (Nebraska State Colleges), or community college governing boards. Prohibits public postsecondary institutions from requiring participation in DEI programs as a condition of employment or enrollment and from spending public money on DEI programs or offices. Preserves activities for legal compliance (offices staffed by attorneys), sexual‑harassment training, grant/accreditation statements, demographic data collection, scholarly research, student organization activities, and short‑term guest speakers. 109-1-LB553_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB553_Intro_Copy.docx LB553 amends the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act to add accredited dietitian nutritionist programs and licensed dietitian nutritionists as eligible for student loans and loan repayment. 109-1-LB554_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB554_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB554 creates the Nebraska Health Professions Commission and explicitly names the chief medical officer of the Department of Health and Human Services (or the chief medical officer's designee) as a member of the commission. 109-1-LB555_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB555_Intro_Copy.docx LB555 (2025) amends the Funeral Directing and Embalming Practice Act to create an "assistant funeral director" credential, define its supervised scope (funeral services, interments, family arrangements, and management of licensed funeral establishments), and require each assistant to have a written collaborative agreement with a licensed funeral director. Licensed funeral directors must supervise assistants and retain collaborative-agreement records. Disciplinary enforcement is to proceed under existing credentialing statutes (e.g., sections 38-178, 38-179, 38-196) and applies to department rules or other regulatory bodies. 109-1-LB559_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB559_Final_Copy.docx LB559 creates new criminal forfeiture procedures and a Financial Fraud Victims' Reimbursement Fund administered by the Nebraska Attorney General. Prosecuting authorities must specifically plead forfeiture in covered financial-transaction indictments; district courts conduct pretrial and post-conviction evidentiary hearings, allow intervention by third‑party claimants, and may appoint counsel or permit in forma pauperis. The Reimbursement Fund consists of assets forfeited from financial transaction offenses, is invested by the State Investment Officer pursuant to the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act, and remains available for 36 months (or until claim resolution). The Attorney General adjudicates victim reimbursement applications and distributes funds (pro rata if insufficient). Remaining funds after the hold period are remitted to the State Treasurer for constitutional distribution. No specific appropriations are included. Creates the Financial Fraud Victims' Reimbursement Fund, to be administered by the Attorney General. The fund consists of assets forfeited from financial transaction offenses (per section 28-1601). The Attorney General will prescribe the application process, determine qualifying losses, award reimbursements (pro rata if requests exceed available funds), and hold funds for at least 36 months or until related applications are resolved. Money in the fund may be invested by the State Investment Officer under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. After the holding period, remaining funds are remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution under the Nebraska Constitution. "Victim" expressly includes individuals and entities, including financial institutions. No specific appropriations or new budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB561_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB561_Final_Copy.docx Department of Transportation - Authorizes the Department of Transportation (DOT), along with the Nebraska State Patrol for interstate routes, to issue special/continuing permits (including new overweight raw‑milk vehicle permits) and to make permit applications available in county treasurers' offices or other locations the DOT selects. \n- Requires DOT to create, publish on its public website, and annually review a bridge map identifying prohibited bridge structures for overweight raw‑milk vehicles (map due before Jan 1, 2026). \n- DOT may revoke overweight raw‑milk permits for violations or if DOT determines permits risk loss of federal aid; revocations are subject to written notice and appeal under the Administrative Procedure Act. \n- DOT may grant vehicle‑length exceptions to meet axle weight limits. \n- DOT may sue to recover costs when an overweight raw‑milk vehicle damages a prohibited bridge; recovered funds are remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Roads Operations Cash Fund. Creates an overweight raw‑milk vehicle permit regime administered by the Department of Transportation (DOT). Key DOT duties and powers: define and publish a statewide “bridge map” by Jan 1, 2026 (annual updates; post to DOT website) identifying prohibited bridges; issue and revoke overweight raw‑milk permits for violations (written notice required; appeals under the APA); authorize limited Interstate travel only with FHWA approval; grant limited vehicle‑length exceptions to meet axle weight limits; revoke all permits if DOT determines federal aid is at risk. DOT may sue to recover bridge‑repair costs when an overweight raw‑milk vehicle damages a prohibited bridge; recovered monies must be remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Roads Operations Cash Fund. Individuals may request revision, repeal, or conversion of guidance to a rule; agencies must respond in writing within 60 days and publish decisions publicly. The bill prohibits agencies from issuing new guidance July 1, 2025–July 1, 2027 except for federal-compliance needs, bars guidance exceeding federal requirements, and revokes guidance/provider bulletins from July 1, 2022–July 1, 2025 (unless federally required) pending rulemaking. The act becomes operative July 1, 2025 and includes an emergency clause making it effective upon enactment. No appropriations or budget changes are included. Prohibits state agencies from issuing guidance from July 1, 2025, to July 1, 2027, unless expressly needed to implement or comply with new federal rules. Mandates that guidance may not exceed federal regulatory requirements. 109-1-LB574_Intro Withdrawn Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB574_Intro_Copy.docx LB574 establishes procedural and workplace protections for certified firefighters and emergency personnel. It defines “complaint,” “formal investigation,” and “interview,” requires investigations be completed in a reasonable timeframe, and mandates a written summary of complaints before interviews. Interviews must be audio recorded; firefighters may have legal or union representation; written investigation outcomes must be provided; complaint materials remain confidential unless disclosure is legally required or consented to; polygraph exams are prohibited; and firefighters may seek damages for false complaints and pursue grievances. The bill also affirms rights to safe working conditions, training, equipment, mental-health services, confidentiality of personal information, off-duty political activity, and access to personnel and training records. No state agencies, departments, or budget appropriations are specified. Adds procedural and employment protections for firefighters (defined to include certified firefighters, emergency medical technicians, and paramedics). Fiscal provisions: initial postcard printing is paid from the county general fund; ongoing creation and mailing costs (including staff time, materials, postage) are charged proportionately to participating political subdivisions based on parcel counts. The act takes effect immediately. At least $100,000/year allocations for a statewide SkillBridge program and $100,000/year for veteran mental‑health community providers are specified.\n\n- Department of Economic Development: Administers the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (receives section 76-903 revenue) and may prioritize Economic Recovery Contingency Fund projects; the Affordable Housing Trust Fund must allocate, from each $1.05 received, at least $0.05 to emerging developers and $0.20 to special population/innovation housing.\n\n- Department of Revenue: Tax Commissioner/stamps administration retained; Department may issue declaratory rulings. The documentary stamp tax ($3.30 per $1,000) allocations from section 76-903 are specified: $1.05 to Affordable Housing, $0.25 Site & Building, $0.25 Homeless Shelter, $0.40 Behavioral Health, $0.05 Economic Recovery, $0.05 Military Installation, $0.05 Innovation Hub, $0.05 Health Care Homes, and $0.40 Child Care Grant Fund. Summary of added provisions (by agency):\n\n- Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS): Establishes a Child Care Grant Fund (receives 40¢ per $1 from sec. 76‑903) to award need‑based grants to licensed child‑care centers and at‑home providers for staff retention/recruitment incentives and capital expenses. DHHS must contract with a statewide organization to manage applications, review, and provide technical assistance. Behavioral Health Services Fund also receives 40¢ per $1; Health Care Homes for the Medically Underserved Fund receives 5¢ per $1.\n\n- Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA): Receives at least $100,000/year to contract with community organizations to create a statewide SkillBridge/veteran attraction program; at least $100,000/year is directed to community providers of veteran mental‑health services.\n\n- Military Department: Military Installation Development and Support Fund receives 5¢ per $1 to support community‑based veteran services (per sec. 55‑901).\n\n- Department of Economic Development: Innovation Hub Cash Fund receives 5¢ per $1 for operations; 5¢ per $1 to an Economic Recovery Contingency Fund to establish/operate an office to pursue and coordinate grant funding statewide.\n\n- Department of Revenue: Implements transfers under sec. 76‑903 according to the new per‑dollar distribution schedule; from each $1.05 transferred at least 5¢ must go to emerging developers and at least 20¢ to special‑population/innovation housing programs. 109-1-LB584_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB584_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services LB584 authorizes courts, when additional information beyond a presentence report is needed before sentencing, to commit an offender to the Department of Correctional Services. 109-1-LB585_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB585_Intro_Copy.docx LB585 amends Section 43-2404.02 governing the Community-based Juvenile Services Aid Program. It preserves a 10% annual General Fund set‑aside (excluding administrative funds) for development/maintenance of a common data set and evaluation—allocations to the commission and the University of Nebraska at Omaha, Juvenile Justice Institute (UNO JJI) are specified—and adds a separate 10% set‑aside for grants to community‑based organizations located in qualified census tracts with annual budgets ≤ $1 million that provide pre‑contact juvenile crime prevention. The remainder of program General Funds is apportioned by a commission formula based on county/tribal youth populations and juvenile justice contact; the commission may require up to a 5% local match. The commission must consult and coordinate with the Office of Probation Administration, juvenile diversion programs, law enforcement, courts, Nebraska Association of County Officials, and UNO JJI, and report annually to the Governor and Legislature. Specifically:\n- Directs that 10% of the Program’s annual General Fund appropriation (excluding administrative budget funds) be reserved for grants to community‑based organizations located in qualified census tracts (per 26 U.S.C. 42(d)(5)(B)(ii)(I) as of Jan 1, 2025) with annual budgets ≤ $1 million, for pre‑contact juvenile crime prevention.\n- Requires grant distribution to consider: staff with lived juvenile‑justice experience, organization budget size, qualified‑census‑tract location, and served population demographics.\n- Assigns the University of Nebraska at Omaha, Juvenile Justice Institute, to help grantees develop logic models and evaluation measures.\n\nNo additional appropriation amount is specified beyond the 10% set‑aside. 109-1-LB586_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB586_Intro_Copy.docx LB586 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §32-944 to require county sheriffs and directors (or designated staff) of county/city jails and detention centers to ensure voting access for individuals unable to vote in person housed at those facilities. It requires a facility plan that: informs restricted individuals of their voting rights and registration/verification options; provides reasonable access to verify/register; designates a jail location for ballot return to be collected by two registered voters unaffiliated with the same party; and establishes a ballot-deficiency cure process. The election commissioner or county clerk must adopt procedures consistent with the Election Act and Secretary of State rules. Noncompliance by a sheriff or facility director is subject to a civil penalty assessed by the district court and payable by the county. No appropriations or funding changes are included. The bill repeals the original section. Adds duties and procedures for county jails/detention centers to ensure eligible incarcerated or “restricted” individuals can verify, change, or register to vote; access voter registration services; return ballots at an on‑site location collected by two registered voters from different political parties; receive information on return methods/locations/deadlines; and have opportunities to cure ballot deficiencies. Assigns operational responsibility to county sheriffs or facility directors/designated staff and requires election commissioners or county clerks to adopt conforming procedures per the Election Act and rules promulgated by the Secretary of State. Noncompliance by a jail/facility is subject to a civil penalty assessed by the local district court and payable by the county. No new appropriations or specific budget allocations are provided. 109-1-LB587_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB587_Intro_Copy.docx LB587 amends Nebraska’s Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (sections 76-1425 and 76-1427). Key changes:\n- Shortens notice/remedy timelines: landlords now have seven days to remedy a material noncompliance (notice of termination must still be at least 14 days after receipt); repeat breaches within six months allow tenant termination on seven days' notice.\n- Expands tenant remedies for landlord failures (including failure to supply water, hot water, heat, essential services, or to remediate mold/pest infestations): tenants may procure and deduct reasonable costs from rent, recover diminution in fair rental value, recover diminution in value of tenant personal property from landlord negligence/deliberation, and—if the failure is deliberate—recover actual/reasonable substitute housing costs. Tenants are excused from paying rent during noncompliance; reasonable attorney fees available.\nNo state agencies, departments, appropriations, or budget changes are referenced. Adds tenant remedies for landlord failure to remediate known mold or pest infestations: tenants may purchase supplies or services to remediate during the landlord's noncompliance and deduct actual, reasonable costs from the rent; and may recover damages for diminution in value of the tenant's personal property caused by the landlord's deliberate or negligent noncompliance. No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriation changes are referenced. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB588_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB588_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill retains and clarifies multiple duties of the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). 109-1-LB589_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB589_Intro_Copy.docx LB589 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79‑1142. Key agencies: the State Board of Education (sets the support‑services percentage cap), the Department (Nebraska Dept. of Education) (administers reimbursements, audits documentation, and reports), the State Treasurer and Director of Administrative Services (certify and draw warrants), and the Governor plus the Legislature’s Appropriations and Education Committees (receive annual reports).\n\nFunding and budget provisions:\n- Department reimburses school districts/cooperatives 80% of allowable excess special‑education costs in the following fiscal year; if General Fund appropriations are insufficient, payments are pro rata and the remainder is paid from the Education Future Fund.\n- The Board’s support‑services percentage cannot exceed (10% minus the Legislature’s set‑aside percentage).\n- Separate set‑asides from special‑education appropriations for services/supports must equal prior year requests plus unpaid amounts.\n- Payments scheduled monthly (minimum seven installments beginning in December).\n- Amounts received under the Extraordinary Increase in Special Education Expenditures Act are subtracted from reimbursements and transferred to the Education Future Fund.\n\nOperational change:\n- Special‑education substitute costs are allowable; districts must provide four days/year of professional leave for special‑education staff, supported by substitutes. Adds that allowable and reimbursable special education costs explicitly include substitute service costs. It requires each school district to provide special education staff four days of professional leave per year, with substitute personnel covering those days; the leave must be used onsite solely to complete essential documentation for students on the staff’s caseload. No specific state agency (e.g., department of education) is named and no dollar amounts, appropriations, or new funding allocations are specified—only that substitute costs are eligible for reimbursement. 109-1-LB597_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB597_Intro_Copy.docx LB597 amends the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act and directs actions by the State Department of Education, Property Tax Administrator, Tax Commissioner/Tax Commission, Director of Administrative Services, Auditor of Public Accounts, Governor, the Legislature’s Appropriations and Education Committees, and the state board.\n\nKey fiscal and administrative changes:\n- Foundation aid (Dept. of Education): through 2024‑25 remains $1,500 per formula student; for 2025‑26 onward equals the greater of $1,500 per formula student or 7.5% of basic funding. Twenty‑four percent of foundation aid is paid from the Education Future Fund. Foundation aid counts as a formula resource at 100% for 2023‑24 and 2024‑25, then 60% thereafter.\n- Local effort rate (affects local effort rate yield): beginning 2025‑26, certification uses the maximum levy less $0.10 (affecting state/local funding shares).\n- Adjusted valuations (Property Tax Administrator/Tax Commissioner): agricultural/horticultural land valuation factor reduced from 72% to 65% for 2025‑26 onward.\n- Certification timing: Dept. certifications and required legislative funding reports set for June 15, 2025, and March 1 annually thereafter; prior certifications for FY2025‑26 are void. Adds provisions effective for school fiscal year 2025-26 and thereafter affecting school finance under TEEOSA. Key points:\n- Foundation aid to each school district = greater of $1,500 per formula student or 7.5% of basic funding (per §79-1007.16).\n- For state aid certification (§79-1022) the local effort rate = the maximum levy authorized under §77-3442(2)(a) minus $0.10.\n- For final state aid calculation (§79-1065) the local effort rate is set so that (rate × total adjusted valuation of taxable property in local systems receiving equalization aid) plus legislative state aid and other local receipts equals total formula need; each system’s local effort yield = its adjusted valuation × that rate.\n- Adjusted valuation for SFY 2025-26 onward is fixed at 65% of actual value (§§77-1359, 77-1363) and 65% of special valuation (§77-1343). 109-1-LB598_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB598_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services References to the Department of Administrative Services (DAS) in LB598:\n\n- Transfers to Education Future Fund: The State Treasurer is directed to transfer $1,000,000,000 (FY2023-24) and $250,000,000 (FY2024-25) from the General Fund to the Education Future Fund "on such dates and in such amounts as directed by the budget administrator of the budget division of the Department of Administrative Services." The bill expresses intent for $250,000,000 annual transfers thereafter.\n\n- Payment certification and warrants: The Department of Education must certify state aid amounts to the Director of Administrative Services. For special education reimbursements, the State Treasurer will notify the Director of Administrative Services of available funds in the General Fund and Education Future Fund, and the Director shall draw warrants against such appropriated funds. Summary (focus: Department of Administrative Services)\n\nThe added provisions require the State Department of Education to accept LEP funding applications by Jan 15 and pay eligible school districts from the Education Future Fund by Jan 31. Eligibility/calculation: take half of the prior-year LEP expenditures, multiply by 107%, and pay the difference between current-year LEP expenditures and that amount. If total awards exceed the Fund balance, payments are reduced proportionally. Beginning 2025‑26, the department must also reimburse districts/cooperatives for additional costs under Section 504 at the same percentage used for special education reimbursement; these payments are supplemental and the department will set reporting rules. 109-1-LB5_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB5_Intro_Copy.docx LB5 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §28‑470 to provide civil, administrative, and limited criminal‑immunity for use, prescribing, dispensing, and administration of opioid antagonists (e.g., naloxone) by specified actors. Covered actors include health professionals licensed under the Uniform Credentialing Act (physicians, physician assistants, nurse practitioners, pharmacists), family/friends (including school personnel), emergency responders licensed under the Emergency Medical Services Practice Act or EMS Compact, and peace officers or law enforcement employees of agencies (police departments, town marshals, sheriffs, Nebraska State Patrol). 109-1-LB600_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB600_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Transportation - Authority to remove: The Department of Transportation (DOT) or its agents may remove vehicles or objects from a highway or highway shoulder without owner consent if they are or could impede traffic; DOT and its agents are immune from liability for damage caused by such removal (sec. 7).\n\n- Temporary speed reductions: DOT may temporarily reduce maximum lawful speeds for weather, traction, emergencies, congestion, etc., must display electronic/digital signs showing the reduced limit and restoration instructions, make reductions in 5 mph increments, keep records of changes and each highway's speed limit, develop/implement policy, and adopt rules (sec. 9).\n\n- Automated enforcement: DOT may enforce school crossing‑zone and highway work‑zone speed limits using speed control enforcement systems, may contract with certified operators, assess civil penalties, and must create guidance to calculate administrative fees (secs. 10, 12, 14).\n\n- Signage and calibration: DOT must erect/maintain signs for the moved‑over law and systems’ images/data are restricted to DOT/local authority use; calibration must be performed by laboratories independent of DOT (secs. 17, 19, 16).\n\nNo funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are specified. Added provisions give the Department of Transportation expanded operational and enforcement authority. Key DOT actions authorized: remove vehicles/objects from highways or shoulders that impede traffic (DOT/agents immune from damage liability); temporarily reduce posted maximum speeds for weather, traction, emergency, or congestion (must display electronic/digital signage, reductions in 5 mph increments, no minimum speed, DOT must adopt policy and keep records); and enforce school-crossing and highway work-zone speeds using speed-control enforcement systems (definition, operator training, annual independent calibration, daily operator logs, confidentiality rules). Enforcement conditions, recording thresholds (school: >6 mph; work zone: >11 mph), owner notice, civil penalties, appeal procedures, and an administrative fee methodology (DOT to publish guidance) are specified. No direct appropriations, budget allocations, or specific funding changes are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB602_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB602_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the "Delete Act" and assigns key implementation and enforcement roles to the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. The Secretary of State must establish (by Jan 1, 2028) and host an accessible deletion mechanism and maintain publicly accessible data-broker registration information. Data brokers must annually register with the Secretary of State (by Jan 31), provide specified disclosures, and pay a registration fee set by the Secretary (not to exceed $300). The Secretary may charge data brokers an access fee to cover reasonable costs. Noncompliance with deletion duties triggers a $200 per-day civil penalty payable to the Secretary of State. The Attorney General may enforce penalties, seek injunctive relief, and recover attorneys' fees. The Secretary of State will select independent auditors for triannual compliance audits and may adopt rules to implement the Act. Violations are added to Nebraska's deceptive trade practices statute.\n\n[NOTE: Budget-related content may be missing from this summary. Please review manually.] Adds recurring roles for the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. Key Secretary of State duties: host publicly accessible data-broker registration info and establish (by Jan 1, 2028) an accessible deletion mechanism with security, accessibility, agent support, and audit/reporting processes; select independent auditors (first audits due by Dec 31, 2030); promulgate rules. Financial provisions: annual data-broker registration fee (set by Secretary, ≤ $300); the Secretary may charge data brokers an access fee to cover the mechanism's reasonable costs; civil penalties ($200/day per missed deletion request) are payable to the Secretary of State. The Attorney General may enforce civil penalties, seek injunctive relief, and recover attorneys' fees and costs. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB603_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB603_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB603 assigns several explicit roles and budget-related duties to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS):\n\n- DHHS will determine the applicable poverty level (up to 300% of poverty) used to set client contribution ranges and must adopt and promulgate the client family income schedule by rule. \n- DHHS may reimburse care management units for costs; reimbursements are to be based on actual casework time units and may include personnel, administration, eligibility review, contractual and support services, and other direct and indirect costs. \n- DHHS must adopt standardized reimbursement rates and adjust them at least every three years. \n- Appropriations for DHHS reimbursement of services (sections 81-2229 to 81-2235) and for DHHS program administration must be made separately from funds under the Nebraska Community Aging Services Act. 109-1-LB604_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB604_Intro_Copy.docx LB604 assigns and clarifies duties and court procedures involving the Secretary of State, the Revisor of Statutes, and Nebraska courts for initiative and referendum petitions. Key provisions:\n\n- Secretary of State: receives filings (sponsor names/addresses), transmits measure to the Revisor, keeps filings confidential five days, posts text/notice when a sample petition is filed, prepares petition form within five business days, and must announce and state reasons if refusing placement on the ballot for legal insufficiency (excluding signature insufficiency); failure to state reasons waives those defenses.\n- Revisor of Statutes: reviews and suggests form/draftsmanship changes within ten business days.\n- Courts: mandamus suits filed in Lancaster County District Court within ten days of refusal; suits asserting insufficiency advanced expeditiously, with appeal to the Court of Appeals within ten days. If a suit does not involve signature insufficiency, the Nebraska Supreme Court may hear the case in original jurisdiction if practicable. Petition sponsor of record is a required defendant. Parties may raise substantive facial insufficiency. \n\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. Adds requirements for the Secretary of State to post the measure text and a notice that it is in circulation on the Secretary of State’s website upon receipt of a sample petition, and to keep that posting up until the petition-filing deadline. If the Secretary of State refuses to place a measure on the ballot for legal insufficiency other than lack of signatures, the Secretary must announce the refusal on the same date as the circulation posting and state the reasons; failing to state reasons waives those defenses. Courts or officials may have a measure declared legally removed if preventing certification/printing is no longer practicable. Lawsuits challenging legal sufficiency (except signature insufficiency) must be filed within 60 days of the circulation posting (or by the petition filing deadline if the 60th day is later); the Nebraska Supreme Court shall hear non‑signature challenges in original jurisdiction if practicable. Parties may raise facial substantive insufficiency at any time; ripeness is not required. No funding or appropriation changes. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB605_Intro Withdrawn Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB605_Intro_Copy.docx LB605 requires each public school board to adopt a policy governing student participation as a transgender student in school-sponsored extracurricular activities and in activities run by any athletics or activities association of which the school is a member. Schools must establish an application process managed by the school administrator or athletic director, require documentation (current registration, written statements from student and parent/guardian, third‑party affirmations of gender identity and expression), and have the school board determine eligibility and, if approved, submit required documentation to the relevant athletics/activities association. Eligibility is defaulted to biological sex on the birth certificate unless approval as a transgender student is granted. The policy must not be construed to promote medical gender‑transition treatments. No funding or appropriations are included. Adds requirements for school boards and school officials (school administrators, athletic directors) to develop and adopt policies governing transgender students' participation in extracurriculars. School boards must: review written requests (including student/parent statements, current registration, and supporting documentation from others), determine eligibility under the local policy and any applicable athletics/activities association rules, and submit/cooperate with associations to obtain association determinations. It specifies that single‑sex teams are determined by biological sex on the birth certificate unless a board approves transgender participation under the policy. The policy must not be construed to encourage medical treatment, and it does not change existing cross‑gender exception rules. Agencies referenced: local school boards, schools/administrators/athletic directors, and athletics/activities associations. No funding or appropriation changes. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB606_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB606_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Revenue The bill transfers parole‑supervision functions to the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), abolishing the Division of Parole Supervision and the Director of Supervision and Services and vesting related powers in the Director of Correctional Services. DCS is given expanded responsibilities to operate and staff facilities, administer parole services, maintain Board of Parole records, set performance metrics, adopt validated risk‑and‑needs assessments, create individualized program/reentry plans, train parole officers, run a technical‑parole‑violation housing pilot, and oversee community work‑release and reentry centers (standards, staffing, approvals, inspections, records, monitoring). Parolees will pay a $25 monthly parole programming fee to the State Treasurer credited to a Parole Program Cash Fund for DCS use. The Legislature intends a $1,000,000 General Fund appropriation to implement the Community Work Release and Reentry Centers Act. DCS staff and contractors must cooperate with investigations; DHHS may access confidential records under DCS subpoena for licensure probes. Employees of DCS and specified Department of Revenue employees are excluded from the definition of law enforcement officer. Department of Correctional Services\n- Added duty to maintain all records and files for the Board of Parole, including records for individuals under lifetime community supervision (section 83‑174.03).\n- Clarifies this does not prohibit the department from also maintaining daily records/files for the Board of Pardons.\n- Adds language tying operational decisions to whether continued in‑facility correctional treatment, medical care, or vocational/other training will substantially enhance an offender’s ability to lead a law‑abiding life after release.\n\nDepartment of Health and Human Services\n- No underlined additions affecting DHHS in the provided text.\n\nDepartment of Revenue\n- No underlined additions affecting the Department of Revenue in the provided text.\n\nFunding/appropriations\n- No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included in the underlined text. 109-1-LB607_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB607_Intro_Copy.docx LB607 designates the Nebraska Department of Environment and Energy as lead agency to implement and enforce extended‑producer‑responsibility and waste‑reduction provisions. The department will promulgate rules (including fees), approve battery stewardship plans, maintain a public program website, audit compliance (appeals to the Environmental Quality Council), and may treat submitted data as confidential or join multistate clearinghouses. Reporting by manufacturers (resin‑by‑resin virgin vs. postconsumer plastic) begins Jan 1, 2027. Civil penalties (initial recycled‑content penalty $0.20/lb; potential price‑differential formula after Jan 1, 2029) are remitted to the State Treasurer; noncompliance can incur up to $1,000/day. Landfill/solid‑waste fees rise to $2.25/ton (2026), $3.25 (2027), $4.25 (2028); revenues split 50/50 between the Integrated Solid Waste Management Cash Fund (spill response, regulation, remediation, monitoring) and the Waste Reduction and Recycling Incentive Fund (department‑administered grants/reimbursements, admin deductions, $1.5M/year scrap‑tire cap through 6/30/2029). The department may set program fees and manufacturer registration fees; act operative Jan 1, 2026. Key agencies: the Department of Environment and Energy (the Department), the Director of Environment and Energy, the Environmental Quality Council, and the State Treasurer.\n\nMajor agency roles and funding/budget items:\n- The Department is the primary implementing, rulemaking, enforcement, and reporting authority for the battery stewardship, minimum recycled content, and related programs. It must adopt rules, set/allocate fees, host an electronic registration system, post data online, and may join a multistate clearinghouse.\n- Fees: battery stewardship organizations pay annual fees set by the Department to cover the Department’s full costs and to allocate costs among organizations. Manufacturers must register annually and pay a $1,000 registration fee (modifiable by the Department).\n- Penalties and remittances: civil penalties (various caps, including $1,000/day and up to $10,000/day for repeat violations) and per‑pound recycled‑content penalties (initially $0.20/lb) are collectible and remitted to the State Treasurer per constitutional distribution. Appeals go to the Environmental Quality Council.\n- Timelines: Dept. must complete and report an assessment of noncovered batteries (due Oct. 1, 2027). \n- Disposal fee schedule added: $2.25 (2026), $3.25 (2027), $4.25 (2028). 109-1-LB609_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB609_Final_Copy.docx LB609 creates the Controllable Electronic Record Fraud Prevention Act and assigns regulatory and enforcement roles to state entities. The bill allows "the department" (as referenced in the Act) to require additional receipt disclosures, request evidence of blockchain analytics use by kiosk operators, and set other compliance requirements. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General must publish model gift‑card fraud notice language; the Attorney General may issue written citations for violations and impose civil penalties up to $250 after an initial warning. The bill amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §29‑817 to explicitly include "controllable electronic records" within the definition of property for search‑warrant law. No appropriations or funding changes are included. Adds regulatory and enforcement duties for unspecified "the department" including authority to require additional receipt disclosures and to request evidence that kiosk operators use blockchain analytics. Requires operators to display and include on receipts contact information for relevant state or local law enforcement and other government agencies for reporting fraud, and to maintain a law‑enforcement contact method. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General must publish model notice language for gift‑card fraud warnings; the Attorney General may issue written citations and impose civil penalties (up to $250 after more than one citation), with the first citation serving as a warning. Also mandates operator compliance officers and antifraud controls. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB620_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB620_Intro_Copy.docx LB620 creates the Neighborhood Revitalization Act. Key government entities and duties:\n- District courts: exclusive jurisdiction for in rem actions to declare a parcel a public nuisance, issue orders of compliance, appoint receivers, establish receiver's liens, and oversee auctions.\n- Municipal corporations (counties, cities, villages): must be notified, may inspect parcels (30-day inspection), may secure/maintain properties and charge costs to owners, and must provide periodic updates to the court.\n- County offices: clerks certify filings; register of deeds/register's office records notices, orders, and receiver's deeds; publication and service follow existing statutes.\n- Receivers: court‑certified persons with authority to take possession, pay operating expenses, satisfy delinquent property tax liens within 30 days, pay municipal fines, and sell parcels at auction. Receiver's liens are first priority except for general property tax liens.\n\nNo appropriations, budget changes, or new funding allocations are included. The added provisions name and empower several government entities: district courts (jurisdiction over in rem proceedings), municipal corporations (cities/townships/counties/villages) and county offices (register's office/register of deeds and the court clerk). Municipalities must be notified, may inspect parcels within 30 days, provide periodic updates to the court, may secure/maintain parcels and charge costs to the owner, and can access parcels if owners fail to act. Filing creates a first-priority receiver's lien recorded in the county register's office (interest per section 77-207). Receivers may pay pre-receivership liens, municipal fines, state and local taxes, and must satisfy delinquent property tax liens within 30 days. Receiver compensation is 10% of expenses (minimum $2,500). Auctions follow statutory sale rules; minimum bid equals the receiver's lien. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB644_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB644_Final_Copy.docx LB644 creates the Foreign Adversary and Terrorist Agent Registration Act and the Crush Transnational Repression in Nebraska Act and assigns primary administration and enforcement duties to the Nebraska Attorney General. The Directors of Insurance and Banking and Finance must accept attestation on their reporting and set filing frequency (not more than annual). Penalties collected (civil fines for violations) are remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution under Nebraska’s constitution. 109-1-LB645_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB645_Final_Copy.docx This bill amends funding and administrative provisions for Nebraska retirement systems.\n\nKey agencies/funds:\n- Retirement Board: continues actuarial certification of state deposits to the School Retirement Fund and Service Annuity Fund.\n- Director of Administrative Services and State Treasurer: State Treasurer transfers certified state deposits on the Director’s warrant from appropriated funds.\n- State Investment Officer: invests Service Annuity Fund pursuant to the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act.\n- Appropriations Committee/Legislature: may review/recommend additional transfers to Class V school districts.\n\nFunding changes:\n- Employee contribution rates to the School Retirement Fund become tiered effective July 1, 2025 (9.75%, 8.75%, 8.0%, or 7.25% based on funded ratio).\n- State contribution previously a flat 2% phases to a funded-ratio–based schedule (2%, 0.7%, or none) beginning July 1, 2025.\n- For Class V systems, from July 1, 2025 the state will transfer 2% of member compensation (plus specified service‑annuity amounts) to Class V districts.\n- Appropriation mechanics remain: transfers drawn from state-appropriated funds as certified. Emergency clause makes the act effective on enactment.\n\nAlso adjusts Nebraska State Patrol survivor benefits (effective dates noted). - Agencies/departments referenced: the state, Class V school districts and their district retirement systems, the School Retirement Fund, and the retirement board (annual actuarial valuation per §84-1503). \n\n- Effective July 1, 2025: employee contribution rates to the School Retirement Fund become a funded‑ratio sliding scale (9.75% if <96%; 8.75% if 96–<98%; 8.0% if 98–<100%; 7.25% if ≥100% of actuarial assets). Deposits are transmitted with employer contributions. \n\n- Beginning in 2025: the state must make additional annual funded‑ratio based deposits into the School Retirement Fund (2.0% of member compensation if funded ratio <96%; 0.7% if 96–<100%; none if ≥100%). \n\n- For Class V districts, the state will annually transfer an amount equal to 2% of member compensation (plus the amount under §79‑966). The Legislature states this does not create new state liability for district funding obligations. \n\n- Effective July 1, 2027: surviving spouse/children benefits are increased to 100% of the officer’s annuity as specified. 109-1-LB652_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB652_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services The bill terminates the Board of Educational Lands and Funds on July 1, 2027, and directs the Department of Administrative Services (DAS) to assume control of all school lands formerly managed by the board on that date. 109-1-LB655_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB655_Intro_Copy.docx LB655 affirms conscience-based refusal rights for health care providers and payors and designates enforcement and reporting channels. It authorizes providers/payors to report alleged violations to the Attorney General, "the department," any state agency charged with protecting medical conscience, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Office for Civil Rights, or other federal agencies. The Attorney General may investigate, administer oaths, take depositions, issue and serve subpoenas, compel evidence, commence civil actions for damages or injunctions, recover attorney fees, and adopt implementing rules and regulations. The bill preserves obligations under state emergency-treatment law and the federal EMTALA. No appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations are included. Adds protections allowing health care providers/payors to report violations to the Attorney General, "the department," any state agency charged with protecting medical conscience, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Office for Civil Rights, or other federal agencies and prohibits retaliation for such reporting or testimony. It authorizes providers/payors to file complaints with the Attorney General; if the AG finds a violation, the AG may bring civil actions for damages, injunctive relief, fees, and use investigatory powers (oaths, depositions, inspections, subpoenas, witness and document compulsion). The AG may promulgate implementing rules. References federal EMTALA (42 U.S.C. 1395dd) and state emergency-treatment obligations. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB656_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB656_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture, Department of Labor, Department of Health and Human Services - Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS): required to apply for SNAP options to maximize federal funding and minimize state General Funds; hire staff to assess options; submit an annual report (by Dec. 1) to the Health and Human Services Committee with program options, actions, caseload, costs and expenditures; develop a USDA Food and Nutrition Service (FNS)-compliant state outreach plan, accept gifts/grants/donations, partner with counties/nonprofits, and submit the plan to USDA FNS for approval and matching funds; may be exempt from implementing the plan if private or federal funds are insufficient; create a TANF-funded categorical eligibility policy raising gross income eligibility to 165% of OMB poverty guidelines through Oct. 1, 2025 and report annually (by Dec. 15) to the committee and Legislative Fiscal Analyst on costs and federal funding availability; prohibited from seeking SNAP work‑requirement waivers and from providing certain federal exemptions; must assign eligible individuals to employment and training programs.\n\n- Department of Agriculture (USDA/FNS): DHHS must submit the state outreach plan to the USDA Food and Nutrition Service for approval and request federal matching funds.\n\n- Department of Labor: referenced as administrator of the SNAP Next Step Program (a DHHS–Department of Labor partnership); eligible SNAP households are encouraged to participate where available; intent that the Department of Labor use no General Funds for these processes and to utilize federal funds if available. Requires the state administering department to not seek or grant SNAP work‑requirement waivers beyond federal law and to assign all persons aged 16–59 to federally defined employment & training (E&T) programs, with listed exemptions (parents of young children/incapacitated persons, half‑time students, certain inpatients, those working ≥30 hrs/week, and some 16–17 year‑olds). \n\nImpacts by agency:\n- Department of Agriculture (USDA/FNS interactions): Limits state waiver requests to USDA; no funding or federal appropriation changes in the text. \n- Department of Labor: Likely increased need to coordinate/provide workforce training and referrals for assigned participants; no new appropriations specified. \n- Department of Health and Human Services (state admin): Primary administrating responsibility and operational workload increase for enrolling/monitoring E&T participants; no funding or budget allocations included. 109-1-LB657_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB657_Intro_Copy.docx LB657 (Judiciary Committee) amends Nebraska Criminal Code section 28-101 to add a new offense, "assault on a sports official." The bill defines "athletic contest" and "sports official" (referee/umpire/linesman or similar who is duly registered by or a member of a local, state, regional, or national organization that provides education/training). An offense occurs when a person intentionally or knowingly causes bodily injury to such an official immediately prior to, during, or immediately after an athletic contest, and knows or reasonably should know the victim is a sports official. The offense is a Class IV felony. The bill repeals the original section 28-101. No state agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations changes are specified. Creates a new crime—assault on a sports official—punishable as a Class IV felony. Defines "athletic contest" to include interscholastic, intercollegiate, amateur, or professional contests, and defines "sports official" as referees/umpires/linesmen (or similar) who are duly registered by or members of local, state, regional, or national organizations that provide education/training to sports officials. The offense requires intentional or knowing bodily injury occurring immediately before, during, or after a contest, with the offender knowing or reasonably knowing the victim is a sports official. No government agencies or departments are specifically named and no funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB658_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB658_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture LB658 amends the Nebraska Pure Food Act and expressly provides powers and duties to the Department of Agriculture. The bill contains no funding, appropriations, or budget allocation changes for the Department of Agriculture. Creates definitions for "agricultural food animal," "cultivated‑protein," "insect‑protein," "plant‑protein," "manufactured‑protein," "identifying meat term," and "qualifying term." Imposes labeling and storage rules: manufactured‑protein products that use an identifying meat term must display a conspicuous qualifying term nearby and be kept and marketed separately from animal‑derived meat at food establishments (distinct shelf tags/representations). Declares such products falsely advertised if these requirements are not met. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB659_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB659_Intro_Copy.docx LB659 requires election commissioners and county clerks to follow new testing, reporting, and security duties when using vote‑counting devices. Agencies/actors and key duties:\n\n- Election commissioners/county clerks: must run at least three independent pre‑count accuracy tests (by the official, a chief deputy or a registered voter of a different party, and the installer/operator); ensure sealing, transport, storage of ballots and device media; adopt procedures for overvotes/damaged ballots (without judging intent), write‑in counting, ballot pickup/transport from drop boxes, and election‑day counting (no tabulation from picked‑up ballots before one hour prior to poll closing); provide appropriate security personnel.\n- County central committees: appoint one watcher per political party; watchers/observers must comply with watcher rules (sec. 32‑1525).\n- Secretary of State: receive and post certification of test completion before statewide primaries/general elections, receive anticipated testing completion dates and written election‑day plans (submitted ≥25 days before each election).\n\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Requires election commissioners or county clerks to run at least three independent pre-count tests of vote‑counting devices (including the counting software), conducted by: the commissioner/clerk; the chief deputy or a registered voter of a different party; and the installer/operator. County central committees may appoint one watcher per political party; other observers only if authorized; all must meet watcher/observer rules and not be excluded unless an unobstructed CCTV view is provided. Election officials must certify testing completion to the Secretary of State (who must post it online) and notify the Secretary of State of the anticipated completion date. 109-1-LB65_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB65_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services The bill affects the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and the Department of Correctional Services (DCS) as follows.
