109-1-LB663_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB663_Intro_Copy.docx LB663 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §23‑114.01 governing county planning commissions and county boards. 109-1-LB664_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB664_Intro_Copy.docx LB664 amends the Administrative Procedure Act. It requires state agencies to solicit public comment (including by newspaper notice) before rulemaking and to allow any person to submit comments or materials in support or opposition electronically or by mail, without requiring travel to a specific location. The bill clarifies judicial review: declaratory-judgment challenges to a rule may be filed in district court in the petitioner’s county of residence, county of principal business, Lancaster County, or the county where the agency’s headquarters is located; the agency must be a party and may not contractually restrict venue. Invalidity grounds include constitutional violation, exceeding statutory authority, or failure to follow statutory procedures (excluding Negotiated Rulemaking Act). Original sections repealed; emergency effective on passage. No appropriations or funding changes. Adds procedural protections for "an agency": agencies must permit anyone to submit comments or supporting/opposing documentation on proposed rules or regulations, allow submissions electronically or by mail, and may not require in-person travel to a specific location. Challenges go to district court in any county with proper venue: the petitioner's residence county, the county of the petitioner's principal place of business, Lancaster County, or the county where the agency has its headquarters. Agencies are barred from taking actions that restrict venue contrary to this section. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB667_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB667_Final_Copy.docx LB667 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-1438 (Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act). It revises dealer compensation rules for diagnostic work and parts: dealers may establish an average parts markup by submitting sequential customer-paid repair orders (or 90 days of orders) for manufacturer audit; manufacturers have 30 days to approve/deny and the board may adjudicate denials (manufacturer bears burden to justify denial under the Act). Manufacturers/distributors may request up to 100 additional repair orders to verify declared rates and may adjust warranty payments if dealer retail rates differ. The bill preserves timelines for dealer warranty claims (file within six months; manufacturers must approve/deny and pay within 30 days), specifies audit and chargeback rights, and reiterates manufacturer recall and warranty obligations. The Legislature repeals the original section. No state agency appropriations or funding changes are included. Added provisions govern franchisor/dealer compensation and rate review under the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act. Key points:\n- Denies use of retail-markup or retail sales data when computing compensation for recommended maintenance services. \n- If a franchisor furnishes parts for warranty work at no/reduced cost, the franchisor must compensate the dealer for dealer cost plus the dealer’s markup, multiplied by the part’s “fair wholesale value,” defined as the greatest of dealer-paid cost, franchisor price-schedule cost, or substantially identical franchisor price-schedule cost.\n- Manufacturers/distributors may request up to 100 additional dealer repair orders (from a 90‑day period within the prior 12 months) to verify declared rates, may adjust warranty payments accordingly, and must allow dealers 30 days to rebut; such requests cannot occur more often than yearly.\n- Parties may mutually agree on rates.\n\nNo government agencies or departments are named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. Hospitals providing emergency care to sexual‑assault survivors must comply with the Act; the department may investigate complaints, hold informal conferences (within 30 days) or formal hearings under department rules, and decisions are appealable under the Administrative Procedure Act. Remedies: first substantiated complaint triggers a written warning and required corrective action; second and subsequent substantiated complaints carry fines of $1,000 either per affected survivor or per month until required training is provided. The bill authorizes department policies to address provider moral/religious objections and contract with peer review organizations; no other appropriations are specified. Adds a complaint-and-enforcement process administered by "the department" (and its director), including use of department representatives and contracted peer review organizations to review alleged failures to comply with the Sexual Assault Emergency Care Act. Complaints may trigger review/investigation; hospitals have 15 days to contest a notice and may request an informal conference (held within 30 days) or a hearing. Timelines: representative's report within 20 working days; department decision within 10 working days; hospitals may request a hearing within 5 working days; department hearings follow its rules and the Administrative Procedure Act and allow subpoenas. Remedies: first substantiated complaint = written warning and required correction; second/subsequent = $1,000 fines (per survivor found denied required info/contraception or $1,000 per month until required training is provided). No appropriations or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB682_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB682_Intro_Copy.docx LB682 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79-770. Issuance of the certificate does not relieve the district’s obligation to continue special education services. 109-1-LB686_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB686_Intro_Copy.docx LB686 prohibits government entities and officials from knowingly maintaining lists, records, or registries of privately owned firearms or their owners, except records kept in the regular course of a criminal investigation, prosecution, or as otherwise required by law. It bars payment card networks from requiring or incentivizing merchant category codes (MCCs) that distinguish firearm retailers, and prohibits covered entities from assigning such distinguishing MCCs. The Attorney General is given exclusive authority to investigate alleged violations, issue written notices, and, if violations persist after 30 business days, file for injunctions; continued noncompliance may lead to civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (stayed pending appeal). Compliance with a statutory MCC requirement is an affirmative defense. No appropriations or budget changes are included. Adds prohibitions and an enforcement scheme centered on the state Attorney General. Key points:\n- Government entities/officials may not maintain lists/registries of privately owned firearms or owners, except records kept in regular criminal investigations/prosecutions or as otherwise required by law.\n- Payment card networks and covered entities may not require, incentivize, or assign merchant category codes that distinguish firearm retailers from other retailers; a statutory defense exists if a code was required by law.\n- The Attorney General has exclusive authority to investigate alleged violations, issue written notices, seek injunctions if violations persist after 30 business days, and pursue civil fines up to $1,000 per violation for noncompliance 30 business days after an injunction. Fines are stayed pending appeal. Remedies are exclusive to this section.\n- No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB68_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB68_Intro_Copy.docx LB68 requires insurers and applicable self‑funded employer plans that cover FDA‑approved, self‑administered hormonal contraceptives to reimburse in‑network providers or dispensing entities on a per‑unit basis: first prescription up to a three‑month supply (if prescribed) and subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply (even if the enrollee was not covered at first fill). The bill amends the Medical Assistance Act (section 68‑901) to direct the department administering the medical assistance program to ensure family‑planning services include a one‑time dispensation of a twelve‑month supply when prescribed. It also clarifies that providers are not required to prescribe twelve‑month supplies and plans may not impose cost‑sharing for switching methods before using a dispensed supply. Insurers must reimburse in‑network providers on a per‑unit basis: first prescription up to a three‑month supply; subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply even if the enrollee wasn’t on the plan at first fill. The bill directs “the department” that runs the state medical assistance (Medicaid) program to ensure a one‑time prescription dispensing a twelve‑month supply. 109-1-LB690_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB690_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Transportation LB690 affects the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and Department of Transportation (DOT) as follows. If plate manufacturing costs exceed the statutory charge, amounts otherwise payable to the DMV Cash Fund are first diverted to the Highway Trust Fund to cover the excess, with any remainder to the DMV Cash Fund. The bill defines “Department” as the DMV under the Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act, requires applicants to submit motorcycle‑safety course proof to the DMV, and directs the DMV to record course completion on driving records by Jan 1, 2024. It also redirects sales/use tax proceeds from aircraft transactions (on/after July 1, 2023) to the DOT Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund. Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV)\n- Adds all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and utility‑type vehicles (UTVs) into the Motor Vehicle Registration Act: they require certificate of title, issuance of license plates under section 60-3,100, and registration when operated on highways pursuant to section 60-6,356. \n- Sets registration fees at $10 for ATVs and $10 for UTVs. \n- Defines UTV technical criteria (≤74" width, ≤180" overall length, dry weight ≤2,000 lb, four+ nonhighway tires) and excludes golf cars/low‑speed vehicles.\n\nDepartment of Transportation (DOT)\n- Clarifies where registered ATVs/UTVs may be operated: allowed on highways generally but prohibited on the Interstate System, state highways, expressways, freeways, and any local ordinance‑prohibited roads.\n\nBudget/funding\n- No appropriations, new funding, or budget allocations are included. 109-1-LB691_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB691_Intro_Copy.docx LB691 requires each public school board and the governing board of any approved or accredited private, denominational, or parochial school that receives state funds to display the Ten Commandments: in each elementary classroom and in each middle‑ or high‑school building. 109-1-LB692_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB692_Intro_Copy.docx LB692 amends the School District Property Tax Limitation Act. It requires the department to compute each school district’s annual property tax request authority using a revised formula: prior-year property tax request (net of any amount that exceeded prior authority) plus prior-year non‑property‑tax revenue (excluding special building fund investment income), increased by the district’s base growth percentage, then reduced by current-year non‑property‑tax revenue (with June 1 data‑gaps defaulting to prior‑year amounts). The department must certify the result to each school board. The bill also allows districts to carry forward unused property tax request authority but expressly excludes carryforward of increases attributable to base growth percentage changes; the department must account for unused authority to school boards. Original sections are repealed. No appropriations or funding allocations are included. The added language applies to school districts: when calculating the current property tax request it requires subtracting any prior-year amount by which the district’s property tax request exceeded its statutory authority under section 79‑3405. It explicitly excludes from that subtraction any increases in request authority that resulted from increases to the district’s base growth percentage under section 79‑3405. No state agencies or departments are named, and no direct appropriations or budgetary transfers are created—this is a technical adjustment to how districts’ property tax requests are calculated. 109-1-LB69_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB69_Final_Copy.docx LB69 revises statutes governing the Commission on African American Affairs. The Commission (14 members appointed by the Governor) must include an immigrant/new American and a young professional among initial appointees; members may serve no more than two full four‑year terms and must have names posted on the Commission website. The bill clarifies the Commission’s purpose (serving African/Black Americans across the diaspora), authorizes it to receive and administer state, federal, and other funds, employ its own personnel, and requires an office for executive management. Duties explicitly include coordinating programs with other state and federal agencies, keeping the Governor’s office apprised, and expanded reporting items — including the Commission’s budget, funding sources, expenditures, grants received, and public funds allocated. An executive board (chair plus four members) may contract for goods/services up to $2,000 per contract and supervise Commission initiatives. Adds initial-appointee requirements: one commissioner must identify as an immigrant/new American and one must be a young professional (18–24). Requires the commission to list all commissioners on its website. Expands the commission's required content/activities to include workforce-development initiatives (scholarships, mentoring, school partnerships), health and wellness programs, criminal justice/public-safety efforts (including police‑community relation improvements and services for formerly incarcerated people), and housing/community development in partnership with housing agencies. Requires metrics/KPIs (employment, graduation, health outcomes, recidivism), public feedback and a community needs assessment, and published future goals/strategic plans. 109-1-LB77_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB77_Final_Copy.docx Department of Insurance, Department of Health and Human Services The bill defines "Department" as the Department of Insurance and directs the Department to approve uniform prior-authorization request forms. Utilization review agents must use forms approved by the Department or may request an exemption from the Department to implement an API or other electronic prior-authorization methodology; agents must notify providers at least 90 days before implementing such electronic systems. The Department of Health and Human Services must make the medical-assistance program's exception-request process readily accessible on its website. The medical-assistance program must cover biomarker testing by January 1, 2028, and contractors must provide testing at equivalent scope, duration, and frequency. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. This act (Ensuring Transparency in Prior Authorization Act) directs the Department of Insurance to regulate utilization review agents: define terms; require website updates and 60‑day provider notice before new/amended prior‑authorization rules; mandate physician or appropriate clinical‑peer adverse determinations and appeals; require notices citing written clinical review criteria and timely clinician discussions; set decision timeframes (with stricter deadlines beginning 1/1/2028); allow exemption from some processes if an electronic prior‑authorization API (per 45 C.F.R. 156.223(b)) is implemented; and empower the department to approve uniform prior‑authorization forms. The Department of Health and Human Services must ensure the medical assistance (Medicaid) program covers biomarker testing by 1/1/2028 under specified clinical criteria, minimize care disruptions, require contractors to match coverage, and post an exceptions process on DHHS’s website. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB78_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB78_Final_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Revenue LB78 (Domestic Violence and Sex Trafficking Survivor Assistance Act) identifies the Department as the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and directs DHHS to administer housing stability programs for victims, including grants, loans, reimbursements, formula-based distribution, contracting with qualified third parties, and—if obligations are met—redistribution of up to 20% excess to certified organizations for housing acquisition/rehabilitation. The Domestic Violence and Sex Trafficking Survivor Housing Assistance Fund is created, administered by DHHS, funded by legislative transfers and public/private sources, and invested by the state investment officer. The documentary stamp tax allocation is amended so that, from each $2.32 collected, $0.07 is credited to the new Survivor Housing Assistance Fund (other allocations specified). The Department of Revenue retains rulemaking/declaratory-ruling authority and may not overturn a county assessor’s sale qualification without its own review. Creates the Domestic Violence and Sex Trafficking Survivor Assistance Act and names the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) as lead. DHHS must promote housing stability for domestic violence and sex‑trafficking survivors by providing grants, loans, rental/utility/security deposit assistance, and provider reimbursements; it may contract with qualified 501(c)(3) nonprofits or tribes. DHHS will allocate assistance by a formula developed with stakeholder consultation and may redirect up to 20% of excess funds toward acquisition/rehabilitation housing for survivors. Establishes the Domestic Violence and Sex Trafficking Survivor Housing Assistance Fund, administered by DHHS, to receive legislative transfers and public/private contributions; funds are investable under state law. No specific appropriation amounts or direct changes to the Department of Revenue’s duties or budget are specified in the added text. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB79_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB79_Intro_Copy.docx LB79 requires a trial court, on a defendant's motion, to dismiss any claim of the defendant’s direct negligence in civil actions involving a commercial motor vehicle (as defined in Neb. Rev. Stat. §60‑316) that requires a commercial driver's license if the defendant stipulates the alleged negligent person was the defendant’s employee or independent contractor and was acting within the course and scope of employment. If those stipulations are made and the employee/contractor’s negligence is found to have caused the damages, the defendant’s liability is limited to respondeat superior. No state agencies or departments are named, and no funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included. Requires that in civil suits involving commercial motor vehicles requiring a CDL, a trial court must dismiss any claim of the defendant’s direct negligence if the defendant stipulates that (a) the alleged negligent person was the defendant’s employee or independent contractor and (b) that person was acting within the course and scope of employment or as the defendant’s independent contractor at the time. If the stipulation is made and that person’s negligence caused or contributed to the harm, the defendant’s liability is limited to respondeat superior. "Commercial motor vehicle" is defined by cross‑reference to section 60‑316. No government agencies or departmental funding or appropriations are mentioned or changed. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB7_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB7_Final_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture LB7 assigns several enforcement and reporting roles to the Department of Agriculture. Restricted entities that meet CFIUS conditions must annually certify compliance to the Department on or before January 15, 2026, and each January 15 thereafter. Any person may notify the Department (or the Attorney General) of violations or suspected violations. The Department is tasked with investigating alleged violations; if the Director has reasonable suspicion, the Director must refer the matter to the Attorney General or outside counsel retained by the Department for enforcement. The Director of Agriculture, together with the Attorney General and retained outside counsel, is charged with determining whether a person is subject to or in violation of the act. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocations are included. Adds a compliance/filing obligation for the Department of Agriculture: restricted foreign persons (nonresident aliens, foreign corporations, foreign governments, or their agents/trustees/fiduciaries) who have either a CFIUS determination that no unresolved national‑security concerns exist or an approved national security agreement must annually certify that status to the Department of Agriculture. First certification is due on or before January 15, 2026, and then by January 15 each year thereafter. No language in the added text changes funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Agriculture. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB80_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB80_Final_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB80 expressly defines "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services in the Child Protection and Family Safety Act and in the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act. It clarifies DHHS responsibilities for child-abuse investigations, alternative and comprehensive assessments, and internal Review‑Evaluate‑Decide teams; requires DHHS to notify and provide written results/notices to investigation subjects and, when applicable, to the Commissioner of Education and appropriate military installations; directs DHHS to negotiate memoranda of understanding with Nebraska military installations addressing information sharing, identification, and confidentiality; and requires DHHS to adopt rules to implement these provisions. No changes to appropriations, funding, or budget allocations for DHHS are included. The added provisions require the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to: contact the family after receiving a child‑abuse/neglect report, identify when the subject is a military family, and notify the appropriate military installation with which DHHS has a memorandum of understanding (MOU). DHHS must negotiate MOUs with each Nebraska military installation that has a Military Family Advocacy Program to establish procedures for identifying military‑family cases, sharing required information, and maintaining state/federal confidentiality. DHHS may adopt rules and regulations to implement these requirements. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB81_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB81_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue - The bill defines "Department" to mean the Department of Revenue (77-6702).\n- The department is tasked with determining the allowable growth percentage used in the Nebraska Property Tax Incentive Act (77-6702(1)).\n- The department must set the credit percentage so total refundable tax credits equal specified amounts: $548,000,000 for taxable years in calendar 2022 and $560,700,000 for calendar 2023; for calendar 2024 the total is the prior-year maximum increased by the allowable growth percentage (77-6703(2)).\n- The department must provide forms and schedules to verify eligibility and allocate school district taxes (77-6703(3)).\n- No direct appropriations or other departmental budget allocations are specified. The added language directs the Department of Revenue to calculate an "allowable growth percentage" equal to the statewide percentage change in total assessed value of all real property from the prior year. For taxable years beginning (or deemed to begin) in calendar year 2024, the department must set the credit percentage so the total credits equal the prior year's maximum credits increased by that allowable growth percentage. No explicit changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB82_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB82_Intro_Copy.docx LB82 adopts the Cosmetology Licensure Compact, creating a multistate regulatory framework administered by a Compact Commission. Key government entities and duties:\n\n- State Licensing Authority (each Member State): retains authority over licensure, scope of practice, investigations, discipline, submission of uniform licensure and investigation data to the Commission Data System, and designation of one delegate (an administrator or designee) to the Commission. \n- Compact Commission and Executive Committee: establish rules, bylaws, budget, a Data System, hire staff, conduct oversight, and handle dispute resolution and enforcement. The Commission may initiate legal action and is entitled to service of process. \n- Financing: Commission may accept grants/donations, levy annual assessments on Member States, charge fees to Licensees (initial and renewal), hire staff, borrow, and establish a budget and financial review. The bill contains no direct state appropriation. Creates an interstate Compact Commission and Executive Committee to administer a multistate cosmetology license. Member States' State Licensing Authorities remain the primary regulators, must cooperate with the Commission, and must submit licensure, adverse action, and investigative data to a Commission‑operated Data System. The Commission may promulgate binding Rules, hold public and closed meetings, initiate or defend litigation (U.S. District Court for D.C. or where its principal office is located), and coordinate dispute resolution. Oversight involves state executive and judicial branches; governors and legislative leaders are recipients of default/termination notices. Funding: the Commission may accept grants/donations, levy annual assessments on Member States (allocated by rule), charge licensee application/renewal fees, borrow money, establish a budget, keep audited financial records, and must secure funds before incurring obligations; an annual financial review by a certified public accountant is required. Law enforcement agencies are authorized to receive/ provide information. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB83_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB83_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill amends the criminal-background-check provision in section 38-131 to require initial-license applicants (including dentists and dental hygienists) to submit fingerprints and to authorize the Federal Bureau of Investigation to release national criminal history record information to "the department." It explicitly defines "the department" for FBI interpretation as the Division of Public Health of the Department of Health and Human Services. Applicants must pay the actual cost of fingerprinting and the background check; the department and Nebraska State Patrol may adopt related cost rules. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Health and Human Services are included. Nebraska adopts the Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact. For the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), acting as the State Licensing Authority, key impacts are:\n\n- DHHS must implement the Compact, issue/monitor qualifying Licenses and Compact Privileges, perform/receive criminal background checks, and report licensure, adverse‑action, and investigative data to the Compact Commission Data System. \n- DHHS retains exclusive authority to impose discipline on Nebraska-issued licenses, may take action based on other states’ investigative information, and must prevent licensees in alternative (nonpublic) programs from using Compact Privileges without authorization. \n- The Compact Commission will set a budget, charge licensee fees, accept grants/donations, and may levy annual assessments on Participating States; DHHS/Nebraska could therefore incur assessment or administrative costs. No specific appropriations or dollar amounts are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB84_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB84_Final_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB84 adopts the School Psychologist Interstate Licensure Compact and amends §38-3113 of the Psychology Practice Act. Pertinent to the Department of Health and Human Services: the amendment permits individuals who performed the referenced duties in institutions accredited by the Department of Health and Human Services (or the State Department of Education or Department of Correctional Services) for two years prior to September 1, 1994, to use the title "psychologist associate" in the context of that employment, limited to specified duties and full-title use. 109-1-LB85_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB85_Final_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles LB85 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §30-24,125 to address title transfers handled by the Department of Motor Vehicles. It requires persons seeking transfer of a certificate of title for a motor vehicle, motorboat, all-terrain vehicle, utility-type vehicle, or minibike to furnish the DMV an affidavit showing applicability and compliance with the statute to obtain a new certificate of title. If ten years have elapsed since an estate closed, the DMV must waive the §30-24,125(a)(5) requirement (showing no pending or granted personal‑representative appointment) when presented with evidence the estate closed and a certified, authenticated copy of the decedent’s death certificate. No funding, appropriation, or budget provisions are included. Adds language allowing, when a certified death certificate is delayed, the use of an "abstract of death" (as defined in §71‑601.01). For the Department of Motor Vehicles, this means an abstract of death can serve as interim proof of death for DMV transactions that require death documentation (e.g., title or registration matters). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB89_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB89_Final_Copy.docx LB89 ("Stand With Women Act") requires the governing body of each public school and public postsecondary educational institution in Nebraska, and applicable private schools and postsecondary institutions, to adopt policies implementing the Act (including visitor/public conduct provisions) that maintain separate interscholastic athletic teams based on the sex definitions set forth. The bill references accrediting bodies recognized by the U.S. Department of Education for postsecondary institutions and affirms that individuals with disorders or differences of sex development retain protections/accommodations under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act. States individuals born with a disorder/difference in sex development receive protections and accommodations under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB8_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB8_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue LB8 assigns administrative responsibilities to the Department of Revenue regarding tax credits. Under the amended Sustainable Aviation Fuel Tax Credit Act, producers must register with the department, provide third‑party certification in forms/manners prescribed by the department, submit applications to the department (which will consider applications in receipt order), and, if qualified, the department will approve and certify the amount of credits to the producer. Producers must attach the tax credit certification received from the department to their tax returns. Separately, the bill makes the residence‑purchase credit subject to recapture by the Department of Revenue if the claimant disposes of or stops using the residence as a primary residence within five years. No appropriations, funding, or budget allocations for the Department of Revenue are specified. Adds the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Tax Credit Act to the list of statutes the Department of Revenue administers, specifies the credit becomes refundable in 2028, and requires the department to process credit applications in the order received. No explicit changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB90_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB90_Final_Copy.docx LB90 amends statutes governing municipal improvement districts in cities of the first class. Key agency actions:\n\n- City clerk must publish notice of district creation in a legal newspaper weekly for at least 20 days. Property owners representing >50% of front footage have 20 days to file written objections; if filed the ordinance is repealed by the mayor and city council.\n\n- The mayor and city council control bidding/material selection: owners representing 25% may petition for materials; bids are postponed 10 days to allow majority selection.\n\n- The mayor and city council determine special assessments, may spread assessments up to 20 annual installments, set interest (not exceeding the statutory rate), and may declare future installments due after three or more delinquencies (with one-time 20-day publication).\n\n- The mayor and city council may issue city bonds (max 20‑year maturity) to fund improvements; special assessments constitute the sinking fund. They may deny district formation where basic infrastructure (water, sewer, street grading) is absent and must notify interested parties in writing. The Legislature’s statutory interest rate (section 45‑104.01) governs limits. Adds that the mayor and city council (specifically of a city of the first class) are responsible for actions relating to creating improvement districts, advertising bids, and authorizing street‑improvement bonds under the cited statutory provisions (secs. 16‑617, 16‑619, 16‑622, 16‑624). Funding language specifies improvements may be paid by levying special assessments on specially benefited property; property owners may prepay the entire assessment within 50 days to avoid liens. The ordinance authorizing bonds governs original bond issuance for district improvements. No new appropriations to other agencies are created. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB91_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB91_Final_Copy.docx LB91 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §70-650.01 governing transfers of electric distribution systems between public power providers and municipalities. It applies to public power districts and public power and irrigation districts and requires conveyance of all right, title, and interest in distribution systems to a city or village upon the municipality's resolution request once bonds are paid or reserves sufficient for redemption exist. Municipal notice, a 30‑day referendum petition process (threshold: signatures equal to 20% of last municipal election vote), and filing with the municipal clerk are retained. In absence of agreement, a city/village may seek a declaratory judgment joined with the district to define “distribution system.” The bill preserves limits on refinancing and debt issuance tied to pledged distribution‑system revenue and permits issuance of bonds for additional facilities. The original section is repealed. Adds the phrase "public power and irrigation district" as a referenced entity. No other government agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations in the provided text. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB92_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB92_Intro_Copy.docx LB92 adopts the "Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act." It requires trial courts to issue orders sealing (granting "clean slate relief" for) eviction records when an eviction proceeding is dismissed. Tenants may petition the trial court to seal records in specified circumstances (including dismissed cases that remain public; reversed, vacated, or unexecuted writs of restitution; nonpayment evictions during the COVID-19 emergency from March 13, 2020–June 30, 2021; cases naming a minor; or judgments violating existing statutory protections), or after three years from a writ or final judgment. Petitions are filed in the trial court, notice is required, parties have 30 days to object, and objections trigger a hearing with the objector bearing the burden. Orders are final and appealable. No state agencies, appropriations, or funding changes are specified. Operative date not provided in excerpt. Creates the Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act (sections 1–6). Defines terms (clean slate relief = sealing under section 5; eviction proceeding; landlord; tenant; residential tenancy; trial court) and incorporates definitions from the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act. Requires the trial court to immediately issue a sealing order under section 5 when an eviction is dismissed. Allows tenants to petition the trial court for sealing immediately in specified situations (e.g., vacated/reversed judgments, writ never executed, COVID-era nonpayment evictions Mar 13, 2020–Jun 30, 2021, named minor defendants, certain statutory violations) or otherwise after three years. Prescribes notice, a 30‑day objection period, hearings if objected (objector bears burden), and makes orders final and appealable. No state agencies or departments are added, and no funding or appropriations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB93_Intro Indefinitely postponed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB93_Intro_Copy.docx LB93 amends Nebraska discovery statutes (sections 29-1912, 29-1913, 29-1918) to expand prosecutorial disclosure and defense access to digital evidence. Key agency roles and effects:\n- Prosecuting attorneys: must disclose reports developed or received by law enforcement agencies that directly relate to investigations, provide names/qualifications/opinions of expert witnesses, and make electronic communication devices, computers, and digital information available for defense testing or analysis.\n- Law enforcement agencies: reports and digital materials created or received by them are subject to discovery.\n- Courts: retain discretion to order time/place/manner for defense testing and to consider safety/coercion concerns; appellate access to sealed prosecutorial showings is preserved.\n- Prosecutorial representatives: negligent or intentional alteration of evidence (beyond necessary testing) can bar the prosecution’s test results from admission.\nJailhouse informants remain governed by sections 29-4701 to 29-4706. No funding or appropriation changes. Adds mandatory disclosure by the prosecuting authority of any expert witness: name, qualifications, and a complete statement of opinions including their basis and reasons. Affirms a continuing duty of disclosure under §29‑1918. Authorizes the trial court to order the prosecuting attorney to provide electronic communication devices, computers, digital information, or their scientific analyses to the defendant or to allow the defendant to conduct comparable tests with defense experts. Defines "computer," "digital information," and "electronic communication device" (cross‑referencing §§28‑1343 and 28‑833). Requires prompt disclosure of newly discovered evidence if it is subject to discovery under §§29‑1912 to 29‑1921 and was previously requested or court‑ordered. Agencies/departments implicated: prosecuting authority/prosecuting attorney, trial courts, and municipal governments (city/village ordinances). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB94_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB94_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor The bill assigns the Department of Labor, in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development, to create and administer digital-skills grant programs: (1) up to $20 million per fiscal year for local education institutions/nonprofits to develop and operate digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts; and (2) up to $20 million per fiscal year for grants covering tuition, materials, transportation, equipment, and child care for low-income individuals. The Department of Labor, with the Department of Economic Development and industry input, must develop standardized, industry-aligned curricula (core skills, special tracks, bootcamps) and partner with employers and tech companies to support apprenticeships and job placement. The Legislature intends to appropriate $50 million annually from the Workforce Development Program Cash Fund to the Department of Labor beginning FY2025-26. The fund’s administration language is amended to include grants under the Act. Summary (focus: Department of Labor; Department of Economic Development)\n\n- The Department of Labor, in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development, must establish two grant programs: (a) up to $20 million/year for local schools/nonprofits to develop and operate digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts; (b) up to $20 million/year to cover tuition, materials, transportation, equipment and child care for low‑income individuals attending those centers. \n- The Labor Department, with Economic Development and industry input, will develop standardized, industry‑aligned curricula (core skills, specialty tracks such as web development, cloud computing, digital marketing, and bootcamps). \n- Labor will partner with tech employers to support apprenticeships, job placement and career progression. Application and priority rules apply if funds are insufficient. \n- Legislative intent: appropriate $50 million annually from the Workforce Development Program Cash Fund to the Department of Labor starting FY2025‑26 for grants under the Digital Skills Empowerment Act. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB95_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB95_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill amends section 68-1206 to direct the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to administer state social services, contract for services, and participate in the federal child care assistance/Subsidy programs. DHHS must provide child care assistance under specified income-eligibility rules; create a child care workforce pilot (Oct. 1, 2025–Sept. 30, 2028); promulgate rules; adopt an annual fixed-rate reimbursement schedule for providers; and submit electronic annual pilot reports (Dec. 1, 2026–2028) including enrollment and monthly expenditure data. Funding: Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) funds shall pay costs from the 2021 income-eligibility changes (July 1, 2021–Sept. 30, 2026), with TANF funds as backup; General Funds may not be used for those costs except for administration. The Department of Health and Human Services must create a pilot program (Oct 1, 2025–Sept 30, 2028) providing child care assistance to the child care workforce under the federal Child Care Subsidy program. Eligibility: household income ≤85% of state median income, an applicant/household member listed in the Nebraska Early Childhood Professional Record System, and working ≥20 hours/week as self-employed or employed at a licensed child care program, Head Start, or Early Head Start; must meet federal non‑income eligibility rules. Enrolled households receive 12 continuous months of assistance without a cost‑share if employment is maintained. DHHS must file annual reports to the Legislature (Dec 1, 2026–2028) detailing enrollment by county/employment type, tenure before enrollment, and monthly program expenditures. No funding or appropriation changes are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB96_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB96_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to submit specified federal Medicaid applications: section 1115 waiver applications as prescribed and other state plan amendments or waivers to CMS. Explicit DHHS duties in amended section 68-911 include submitting amendments/waivers to cover community-based secure residential and subacute behavioral health services; making certain school-provided services directly reimbursable; providing coverage for continuous glucose monitors (by Jan 1, 2023) with eligibility expanded Aug 1, 2024; seeking approval to extend postpartum coverage to at least six months; and, by Oct 1, 2025, submitting a waiver or SPA to designate two medical respite facilities and reporting annually. Funding: up to $600,000 annually is intended from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund for CGM expansion; medical respite services are funded from that same fund. 109-1-LB97_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB97_Final_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles LB97 reorganizes DMV fee authority and fund allocations and creates two new DMV funds. It (1) establishes the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund (administered by the DMV director) and a DMV Ignition Interlock Fund, (2) directs specific fees—including a $10 identification‑inspection fee, NMVTIS reporting fees charged to wrecker/salvage dealers (capped at reporting cost), mailing/postage for plate delivery, and portions of operator’s license/ID, commercial license, ignition interlock, and 24/7 permit fees—to be credited to those funds or to county funds as specified, (3) shifts license‑plate production fee receipts to the License Plate Cash Fund beginning with the 2029 plate cycle (previously to the Highway Trust Fund), and (4) authorizes DMV to collect fees, issue credentials (including electronically), adopt ignition‑interlock rules, administer indigent payments from the Ignition Interlock Fund, credit receipts to the Motor Carrier Services Division Distributive Fund, and allows legislative-directed transfers of DMV Cash Fund balances (including to the General Fund or the Vehicle Title & Registration System Replacement and Maintenance Cash Fund). Investment earnings on the DMV Cash Fund are credited to the General Fund beginning Oct. 1, 2024. Key DMV additions:\n- Defines "amphibious vehicle" and exempts such vehicles from specified statutory sections if validly registered under the Motor Vehicle Registration Act.\n- Title rules: tighter bonded-certificate requirements—applicants must send certified‑mail notice to lienholders; unresponsive lienholders have 30 days and issuance extinguishes liens.\n- Identification inspections: $10 fee per inspection, remitted to State Treasurer for credit to the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund; no fee when a U.S. Government Certificate to Obtain Title is presented.\n- Registration options: allows annual or 2‑ or 3‑year multiyear registrations (implementation by director on/before Jan 1, 2029); multiyear renewals pay fees/taxes for each year.\n- License plates: one plate generally issued/displayed; department may mail plates/registration and charge a postage/handling fee (remitted to DMV Cash Fund). Beginning with 2029 plate cycle, related fees remit to the License Plate Cash Fund.\n- Ignition interlock: DMV must review records to determine applicant eligibility and prior convictions before issuing permits. 109-1-LB98_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB98_Final_Copy.docx LB98 amends statutory definitions of "all-terrain vehicle" and "utility-type vehicle" in the Motor Vehicle Certificate of Title Act, the Motor Vehicle Registration Act, and the Nebraska Rules of the Road by revising size, tire-count, and passenger-design criteria across sections 60-103, 60-135.01, 60-305, 60-358.01, and 60-6,355. It continues to forbid registration of modified or retrofitted ATVs/UTVs that include equipment beyond statutory requirements, repeals the original sections, and takes effect immediately under an emergency clause. No state agencies or departments are named and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. The added text consists only of fragmentary subsection markers and the conjunction "and" — "(3) and (3) and (iii) and." It does not reference any government agency or department, nor does it include any changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB99_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB99_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services LB99 amends provisions of the Nebraska Treatment and Corrections Act to (1) expressly define "Department" as the Department of Correctional Services and "Director" as the Director of Correctional Services (plus related committed-offender and facility definitions) and (2) require the Department to adopt and promulgate Administrative Procedure Act rules establishing levels of restrictive housing, individualized transition plans, and criteria/procedures for placement. The bill limits restrictive housing to 15 consecutive days, defines restrictive housing as under ten hours out-of-cell per day, prohibits placement of vulnerable populations in restrictive housing except for temporary segregation pending classification, and directs the Department to develop secure mental-health housing with meaningful access to social interaction, exercise, stimulation, and therapeutic programming. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocations for the Department are included. Added provisions limit use of restrictive housing: inmates may not be held in restrictive housing for more than 15 consecutive days and (subject to a referenced ten-hours-per-day provision) no more than one inmate may be placed in a single-occupancy cell unless all affected inmates voluntarily agree in writing. The amendment also adds statutory definitions relevant to placement decisions: “developmental disability” (per section 71-1107), “serious mental illness” (a biologically based brain disorder that substantially limits life activities, listing examples such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, OCD, etc.), and references traumatic brain injury. No direct changes to Department of Correctional Services’ funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included in the added text. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB9_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB9_Final_Copy.docx LB9 expands state regulation to cover nicotine analogues, alternative nicotine products, and electronic nicotine delivery systems. Key agencies and changes:\n\n- Tax Commissioner / Cigarette Tax Division: broadened reporting, audit, deficiency-notice, license suspension/revocation, and enforcement authority (including seizure/forfeiture of contraband tobacco products without warrant). May hire inspectors/clerks with Governor's advice and consent and use AG, county attorneys, sheriffs, or other peace officers for enforcement.\n- Attorney General: may seek injunctions, calculate escrow shortfalls, recover investigation costs and fees, and issue enforcement notices.\n- Governor: sets compensation for Tax Commissioner employees.\n- State Treasurer: receives remitted profits as ordered by courts.\n- Federal interaction: requires manufacturers/importers to provide Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau or Customs reporting or 6103 consent.\n\nBudget/funding: administrative enforcement expenses paid by warrants against the General Fund, capped at 4% of collections. New taxes imposed on ENDS and alternative nicotine products (specified per‑unit and percentage rates). Operative January 1, 2026. Adds definitions linking "alternative nicotine product" and "nicotine analogue" to section 28-1418.01 and defines "nicotine analogue." Expands Tax Commissioner authority under the Tobacco Products Tax Act: examine returns, notify of deficiencies (notice deadlines—generally 3 years; 6 years for fraud/omission), and accept written extensions of the assessment period. Imposes a 20% tax on alternative nicotine products based on the first owner's purchase price or the first owner's sale price if manufactured by that owner. Grants enforcement powers: seize contraband tobacco without a warrant; direct return when no willful tax evasion; require forfeited items be destroyed or used for law enforcement then destroyed; assess seizure/destruction costs to the owner; suspend/revoke licenses (sections 28-1420–28-1429) after notice/hearing and impose administrative penalties up to $5,000. Appeals governed by the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes. DOCX | PDF
LB319_Intro_Copy.docx Unknown session Legislative Bill 319 delegates several responsibilities to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). The Department is tasked with maximizing federal funding to minimize the use of state General Funds for SNAP and is required to employ necessary personnel to explore available federal options for Nebraska.\n\nAdditional provisions include the development of a state outreach plan conforming to the Food and Nutrition Service's criteria, which is part of the United States Department of Agriculture. DHHS may seek gifts, grants, or donations to fund the outreach initiative, which must be submitted to the Food and Nutrition Service for approval. If approved, it may secure federal matching funds, aiming to supplement state funds for increased caseloads due to the outreach plan implementation.\n\nThe bill explicitly prohibits the use of General Funds by the Department of Labor for any action regarding a SNAP benefit partnership program, focused on encouraging higher employment among recipients. This program requires no state General Funds but may act with federal or other non-state funding. \n\nLastly, the DHHS is mandated to provide annual reports detailing the efficiencies and costs of these implementations to the Health and Human Services Committee of the Legislature. The legislative text modifies eligibility criteria for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) related to individuals convicted of felonies involving controlled substances. According to the new provisions under 21 U.S.C. 862, individuals convicted of such felonies will now be eligible for SNAP benefits only if they have either completed their sentence or are currently serving parole, probation, or post-release supervision. This change pertains to policies administered by the Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP. The amendment does not include any direct changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations within the specified departments. —
